title: feat(cnm): answer the community's consent requests from the CLI (VTI-APV-014)
body:
Making or widening an unrestricted administrator at the VTC needs another
unrestricted administrator's consent (VTI-APV-014), but only a device
enrolled to handle the task-consent push could answer. An approver with a
cnm profile had no way to sign a decision.

`cnm consent {show,approve,deny} <file|->` takes the request the
requester relays (the refusal body, its `details`, or a bare request
document), picks the one addressed to this profile, and verifies it. The
VTC must have signed it, it must be addressed to this approver, and it
must not have expired. Approving requires typing the requester's match
code (or `--match-code`); a mismatch sends nothing. The decision is
signed with the profile's key under assertionMethod and posted to the
document endpoint.

The approver's shared half is a new `vta_sdk::task_consent` module:
`match_code`, `ConsentRequest::verify` returning a
`VerifiedConsentRequest` (the only type a decision can be built from),
and `decision`. `vtc-client` gains `decide_task_consent`.

It also fixes a mismatch between the two screens: the requester prompt
in `vta_cli_common::consent` printed the whole `zQm…` digest as the
"code", while approver devices show six hex characters of the decoded
digest. Both now call `vta_sdk::task_consent::match_code`, and so does
`vta-mobile-core`, which drops its copy.

Tested end to end in `unrestricted_admin_consent`: a real VTC-signed
request verifies through the SDK, is refused when it is addressed to
someone else, comes from another issuer, or has been tampered with, and
the decision built from it grants the consent.

title: security(resolver)!: one bounded DID-document cache per node, re-resolved once before a verification fails (VTI-KEY-134)
body:
## Problem

- **The VTC had two independent DID-document caches.**
  - The app resolver, built in `server.rs` `init_auth`.
  - A second cache the messaging TDK built for itself (`messaging.rs` `build_messaging`), because it was handed no resolver.
  - Both ran on the SDK defaults: 300 s TTL, 100 entries.
  - Every DIDComm and TSP message on the mediator socket was checked against a cache that the REST and Trust Task paths could neither see nor evict.
- **No cache was refreshed on a verification failure.** A peer that rotated (VTI-KEY-122) looked like a forger until its entry aged out.
- **The TTL was implicit.** No setting reached it, and it is the only thing bounding how long a key revoked for compromise (VTI-KEY-123, no overlap) keeps verifying.

The VTA already shared one resolver across auth and messaging, but its TTL was the implicit default too.

## Change

Spec basis: the key-roles chapter, trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#42 (VTI-KEY-060, 062, 122, 123, 134).

**Bounded, explicit TTL (`[did_cache]`, both nodes).**
- `vti_common::config::DidCacheConfig` has two settings:
  - `ttl_secs`: default **60**, refused at load outside **1..=300**.
  - `capacity`: default 1000.
- The VTA (`vta-config`) and the VTC (`vtc-service/src/config.rs`) read the same type.
- Why 60 s:
  - The TTL governs *revocation* latency only. A compromised key keeps verifying here for at most a minute after it is removed from the document.
  - It costs one resolution per active mutable DID per minute.
  - New keys do not wait on the TTL (see the next section).
  - 300 s, the SDK default and today's behaviour, is the ceiling.
  - `did:key` and `did:peer` are immutable and are not subject to the TTL.
- `vta_sdk::resolver::build_verifier_did_cache_config(url, ttl, capacity)` builds the resolver with the webvh host policy the VTA already used. The VTC now gets that policy too.

**One cache per node.**
- VTC: the messaging TDK is handed `AppState.did_resolver`.
- VTA: the no-app-resolver fallback in `messaging/service.rs` now gets the same bounds instead of SDK defaults.

**Re-resolve once, fresh, then fail closed (`vta_sdk::did_refresh`, new).**

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| `resolve_for_vm` — used by `TrustTaskVmResolver` (every Trust Task proof, both nodes) and the VTC `DidVmResolver` (credential / VP / VRC verification) | A cached document that does not list the method a proof names is re-resolved once before refusal (VTI-KEY-134) |
| `verify_trust_task_proof_with` | If verification fails and the signer's document was served from cache, evict it and verify once more. This covers a key id kept with its material replaced. |
| `unpack_refreshing_sender` — REST DIDComm `auth/authenticate` and `auth/refresh`, both nodes | On authcrypt unpack failure, evict the sender named in the JWE protected header's `skid` and retry once |

Forced refreshes are **rate-limited per DID** (`FRESH_RESOLVE_MIN_INTERVAL` = 5 s, at most 4096 DIDs tracked). A failing proof is attacker-controlled input, and without the floor every bad proof would make this node fetch a third party's DID document. A document fetched for the current call is never refetched.

## Breaks

- Mutable DID documents are cached for 60 s instead of 300 s, so there is somewhat more resolver traffic.
- A `[did_cache] ttl_secs` of 0 or above 300 now **fails config load** on both nodes.
- The VTC messaging listener no longer has its own cache.

## Refresh flood hardening (review follow-up)

- A forced re-resolution after a failed unpack considers only a sender whose document was cached before the first attempt. An uncached or over-long (>1000 byte) `skid` gets no retry and takes no rate-limit slot, so a junk message costs one fetch, not two, and cannot fill the refresh floor.
- When the floor is full, expired entries go first, then the oldest, so a genuine refresh of a cached DID is never refused.
- With `resolver_url`, the revocation window is the local TTL plus the remote resolver's own TTL; this is now stated in the config docs and deploy examples.

## Not covered (follow-ups)

- **Inbound DIDComm on the mediator socket.**
  - The ATM unpacks inside the SDK's live stream, so there is no retry hook. It does now share the node's bounded cache.
  - TSP already evicts and re-resolves inside the SDK (`refresh_vid`, rate-limited).
- **VTI-KEY-060, document-stated validity.** The SDK's moka TTL does not read a validity period from the resolution result. The configured TTL is the only bound.
- **Hand-rolled resolve-then-verify sites not moved onto the helper:**
  - VTC: `members/rotate.rs`, `members/personhood.rs`, `relationships.rs` (×2), `vti-common` SIOP.
  - VTA: `operations/vault/upsert.rs`, which is the sealed-secret authcrypt unpack.
  - These still fail closed on a stale document, but do not re-resolve.
- **Network mode.** `remove` clears only the local cache, so a remote resolver may still answer from its own.

- A deactivated `did:webvh` is still served as its last document by the resolver cache SDK, and a document whose `id` differs from the requested DID sets the cache expiry. Upstream fix in affinidi-did-resolver to follow.

## Tests

- `vta-sdk` `did_refresh`:
  - A cached document missing the method is re-resolved.
  - The forced refresh is rate-limited per DID.
  - The claimed sender is read from the protected header, and anoncrypt names none.
- `vti-common`: the default is bounded and valid; 0, 301 and 86400 are refused.

title: security(resolver)!: one bounded DID-document cache per node, re-resolved once before a verification fails (VTI-KEY-134) (#1737)
body:
security(resolver)!: one bounded DID-document cache per node, re-resolved once before a verification fails (VTI-KEY-134) (#1737)

* security(resolver)!: one bounded DID-document cache per node, re-resolved once before a verification fails (VTI-KEY-134)

The VTC ran two DID-document caches: the app resolver built in
`init_auth`, and a second one the messaging TDK built for itself
because it was given none. Both used the SDK defaults of a 300 s TTL and
100 entries. Every DIDComm and TSP message on the mediator socket was
checked against a cache the REST and Trust Task paths could not see or
evict. Neither cache was ever refreshed when a verification failed, so
a peer that rotated was refused as a forger until its entry aged out.

Bounded TTL (key-roles, dtgwg-vti-spec #42: VTI-KEY-060/062/122/123/134):

- A new `[did_cache]` section (`vti_common::config::DidCacheConfig`)
  holds `ttl_secs` (default 60, refused outside 1..=300) and `capacity`
  (default 1000). The VTA and the VTC read the same type.
- The TTL is what bounds how long a key revoked for compromise keeps
  verifying: VTI-KEY-123 allows no overlap, and nothing else notices a
  removal. A new key does not wait on the TTL, because of the refresh
  below. 60 s caps the revocation window at a minute, for one resolution
  per active DID per minute. 300 s, the SDK default and the old
  behaviour, is the ceiling.
- `vta_sdk::resolver::build_verifier_did_cache_config` builds it, with
  the webvh host policy the VTA already used. The VTC now uses that
  policy too, so the private-host opt-in reaches it as well.

One cache:

- The VTC messaging TDK is handed the app resolver.
- The VTA already shared its resolver. Its fallback when there is no
  app resolver now gets the same bounds, not the SDK defaults.

Re-resolve once, then fail closed (`vta_sdk::did_refresh`):

- `resolve_for_vm`: when a cached document does not list the method a
  proof names, re-resolve it fresh once. This covers every Trust Task
  proof on both nodes (`TrustTaskVmResolver`) and the VTC credential/VP
  resolver (`DidVmResolver`).
- `verify_trust_task_proof_with`: when verification fails and the
  signer's document came from the cache, evict it and verify once more.
  This covers a key id kept with its material replaced.
- `unpack_refreshing_sender`: when an authcrypt unpack fails, evict the
  sender named in the protected header (`skid`) and retry once. It is
  used on the REST DIDComm auth and refresh paths of both nodes.
- Each forced refresh is rate-limited per DID (5 s, with at most 4096
  DIDs tracked). A failing proof is something anyone can send, and
  without the limit each one would make this node fetch a third party's
  document.

BREAKING CHANGE: mutable DID documents (did:webvh, did:web) are cached
for 60 s, not 300 s. A `[did_cache] ttl_secs` above 300 or equal to 0
fails config load on both nodes. The VTC messaging listener no longer
has a cache of its own.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(resolver): refresh only a cached sender, and never refuse a genuine refresh

The forced re-resolution after a failed unpack now considers only a sender
whose document was in the cache before the first attempt. An uncached or
over-long skid gets no retry and takes no rate-limit slot, so a junk message
naming a new DID costs one fetch, not two, and cannot fill the per-DID
refresh floor. When the floor is full, expired entries go first and then the
oldest, so a genuine refresh of a cached DID is never refused.

Document that with resolver_url the revocation window is the local TTL plus
the remote resolver's own TTL.

title: feat(vtc): member pushes follow TSP > DIDComm > REST, with escalation (VTI-TRN-042)
body:
Every Trust Task the VTC pushed to a member (removal notices, task-consent requests, granted notices) went out over DIDComm, whatever the recipient advertised. The workspace rule is that the DID document is authoritative and the transport is the highest-preference one both parties speak: **TSP > DIDComm > REST**. This PR makes the VTC follow that rule for pushes.

This is the Phase B flip for VTC Trust Task pushes, which `docs/05-design-notes/tsp-enablement.md` §14 Q4 had deferred. The note is updated to match.

## How it works

`member_push::push_trust_task(state, recipient, signed_doc, deliver_by)` replaces the DIDComm-only send at all three call sites.

**Selection**
- The recipient's DID document is resolved and matched on service `type`, never on the `#id` fragment.
- REST counts only for `TrustTaskHTTPS`, the one service type that claims to accept Trust Task documents (HTTPS binding 0.2 §6.2). A `VTARest` application API does not count.
- A recipient that advertises nothing, such as a `did:key` wallet, still goes over DIDComm through the shared mediator, as before.

**Durable on the existing outbox (VTI-TRN-030)**
- DIDComm is packed and queued exactly as before.
- TSP and REST are two new named transports, each with its own `drain_loop_via`:
  - **TSP** is sealed at send time. If the recipient is on our mediator, it is routed and returns the `hop_id` the mediator lists it under, so the existing outbox poll records collection. If the recipient is behind another mediator, it is nested. A relationship the peer lost is re-established before sending.
  - **REST** sends `POST {base}/trust-tasks` with the signed document as the body. No bearer token is sent; the document's own proof authenticates it (binding §2).

**Nothing readable at rest**
- A TSP or REST outbox entry carries only the push id.
- The document lives in a new `member_pushes` keyspace, encrypted under the storage key like the install and passkey stores, and excluded from backup.

**Evidence and escalation (VTI-TRN-040, -041, -042)**
- A collected message (class 3), or a REST 2xx from the recipient's own server (class 2), records the push as delivered, with the evidence class.
- An attempt with no evidence in its window re-resolves the recipient and moves to the next transport it offers.
- Each attempt except the last gets its share of the deadline, capped at an hour. A 15-minute consent request therefore tries each of three transports for about five minutes, and a 30-day removal notice tries TSP and DIDComm for an hour each.
- When nothing is left, the push is marked failed and logged for the operator.
- Recipients deduplicate by the document `id`, which every attempt carries unchanged (VTI-TRN-043).

**Not moved**
The credential-exchange protocol messages (offer, issue, query, request-VMC) have no TSP or REST binding, so they stay DIDComm on `AppState::send_to_member`.

## Tests

- **New:** `tests/member_push_didcomm.rs` (`didcomm-harness`), run through a real mediator:
  - **TSP, end to end:** a peer advertising only `TSPTransport` receives the signed document over TSP (binding envelope off), and the push settles delivered over TSP on the mediator's `collected` evidence (class 3). The peer uses the new `TestTspPeer` harness peer, which receives the way the VTC does and accepts the relationship invite. `register_tsp_peer` keeps it offline until the VTC has seen the message waiting, because a collection only counts once it has been observed queued;
  - a REST-only peer receives the document by POST, and the push is recorded delivered with `reply` evidence;
  - a DIDComm attempt with no evidence escalates to REST inside its share of the deadline;
  - an unrecognised service type falls back to the shared mediator.
- **Unit:** selection by service type, only `TrustTaskHTTPS` counting as REST, and a service-less document advertising nothing.
- **Still green:** the `removal_notice_didcomm` and `consent_granted_didcomm` harness tests, plus `unrestricted_admin_consent`, `removal`, `members_crud`, `emergency_bootstrap` and `passkey_state`. The keyspace census is now 40.
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets` with `--features didcomm-harness` and with `--no-default-features`, and `cargo fmt --check`: clean.

## A race the TSP test found

`queue_attempt` writes the push record before the outbox entry. A sweep landing between the two read the missing entry as "no evidence", and with no transport left it recorded a push failed that had never been tried.

A missing entry now waits `ENQUEUE_GRACE` (30s). After that it means the enqueue never happened, for example because the process died between the two writes, so the same attempt is queued again instead of given up on. The sweep also logs why it gives up on an attempt: the outbox state, whether it expired, and whether it was ever seen waiting.

**Running these on a laptop:** the outbox deadlines are wall-clock and the test timer is not, so a machine that sleeps mid-run fails them spuriously. Run them under `caffeinate -i`.

title: Record how the one-key node identities diverge from key roles
body:
Follow-up to #42. This adds divergence-register entries for the key-role requirements that #42 proposes. Requirement changes and register entries are kept in separate PRs, so this PR changes only Appendix F. **It depends on #42**: the requirement IDs it cites are defined there. It should merge after #42, or be rebased if #42 changes those IDs.

### What it adds

A new **Appendix F.6, Key roles and custody**, with eleven rows. Ten are *observed*, against OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure at `e7b06178`. One is *open*. As F.8 asks, the rows describe behaviour and do not name the implementation. The commit message gives the source citations.

| Requirements | Divergence |
|---|---|
| KEY-070, 071, 080, 081, 091, VTC-040 | One Ed25519 key sits in both `assertionMethod` and `authentication` and signs everything the community node signs. The optional ML-DSA-44 key, which falls back to Ed25519, is in `assertionMethod`. This is a legacy identity under KEY-140. The resolution sets the order in which the rows have to close. |
| KEY-090, 092, 094, 150 | No `keyRoles` property exists. Fragments are positional. |
| KEY-145, VTA-008 | The VTA's own identity has the same one-key shape. |
| KEY-110, 111, 115, VTA-008, VTA-033, VTC-041 | The service process holds every private key, from its provisioning bundle, and signs its own credentials and status lists. |
| VTA-009, KEY-111 | The VTA's general signing operation adds a domain tag and cannot produce a Data Integrity proof as the node. No operation or Appendix C capability exists to sign an attestation artefact. |
| KEY-093, 113 | The genesis log's update key is the Ed25519 signing key. Where the committed next keys are held was not established. |
| KEY-114 | The install-token, audit-chaining and storage keys are derived from the signing key. |
| KEY-112, VTC-043 | The backup export includes the key bundle. |
| KEY-100, 101 | No verifier checks `proofPurpose` against the verification relationship. A fix is in progress. |
| KEY-101, 102 | The member client does not verify proofs on the credentials it is issued. A fix is in progress. |
| KEY-120 – 125 *(open)* | The VTA's key rotation is being inspected. No behaviour is claimed yet. |

Adding the section renumbers Closed to F.7 and *How to add an entry* to F.8. The one in-text reference to Closed is updated to match. No requirement text changes.

`npm run render` completes. `docs/index.html` shows the new section with eleven rows of four cells.

title: Record how the one-key node identities diverge from key roles (#43)
body:
Record how the one-key node identities diverge from key roles (#43)

Eleven entries in a new Appendix F.6, recording how the current
implementation diverges from the key-role requirements proposed in #42
(VTI-KEY-070 to VTI-KEY-153, VTI-VTA-008, VTI-VTA-009, VTI-VTA-033,
VTI-VTC-040 to VTI-VTC-043). Ten are observed, against
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure at e7b06178. One is open. The
rows describe behaviour without naming the implementation, as the
register asks. The citations are here.

- Identity shape (KEY-070, 071, 080, 081, 091, VTC-040). The vtc-host
  template (vta-sdk/templates/vtc-host.json) lists #key-0 Ed25519 in
  assertionMethod and authentication, #key-1 X25519 in keyAgreement,
  and #key-2 in assertionMethod only. #key-2 is ML-DSA-44, or Ed25519
  as a fallback. #key-0 signs everything the VTC signs.
- keyRoles (KEY-090, 092, 094, 150). No template carries it. Fragments
  are positional.
- The VTA's own identity (KEY-145, VTA-008) has the same one-key shape.
- Custody (KEY-110, 111, 115, VTA-008, VTA-033, VTC-041). The VTC
  process holds every private key from its bundle and signs its
  credentials and status lists itself.
- Signing path (VTA-009, KEY-111). The VTA keys/sign operation adds a
  domain tag and cannot produce a Data Integrity proof as the VTC. No
  Appendix C capability exists for it.
- Update authority (KEY-093, KEY-113). The genesis webvh updateKeys is
  #key-0's public key. The template defaults to preRotationCount 2. It
  was not established where the committed keys are held.
- Derived secrets (KEY-114). The install-token key, audit key and
  storage key are HKDF-derived from the #key-0 private key
  (vtc-service/src/install/token.rs, server.rs).
- Backup (KEY-112, VTC-043). The VTC backup export includes the key
  bundle.
- Purpose check (KEY-100, 101). No verifier checks proofPurpose against
  the relationship. A fix is in progress.
- Holder (KEY-101, 102). The openvtc client does not verify proofs on
  the credentials it is issued. A fix is in progress.
- Rotation (KEY-120 to 125), open. VTA rotate-keys is being inspected.

Adding a section renumbers Closed to F.7 and How to add an entry to F.8.
The one in-text reference to Closed follows. No requirement text
changes.

title: Separate a node's attestation keys from its operational keys
body:
A VTA or VTC identity today publishes one Ed25519 key in both `assertionMethod` and `authentication`. That key signs every credential and status list the node issues, every message and Trust Task response it sends, and the identifier's own `did:webvh` log, and the service process holds it. VTI-KEY-020 to VTI-KEY-022 require purposes to be stated and checked, but nothing maps a purpose to a relationship, so a verifier cannot tell which key should have signed what. If the most exposed process is compromised, the attacker can forge the community's decisions, including a status list that un-revokes every suspended member.

This PR adds a **Key roles** section to *Identity, DIDs and Key Management*. VTI-KEY-030 gains an exemption for attestation and update keys; other existing requirement text is unchanged; notes point from KEY-020..022 and KEY-040..043 to the new material.

### Requirements added

| IDs | Subject |
|---|---|
| VTI-KEY-070 – 075 | Extensible registry of key roles: `attestation` (assertionMethod only, VTA-held, non-exportable), `operational` (authentication only, may be held by the service), `messaging` (keyAgreement), `update` (the method's update authority, never a VM). One role per key, no material reused across roles or identities, unknown roles confer nothing, capability relationships stay empty. |
| VTI-KEY-076 – 077 | Companion services (for example a forge bridge) have their own DID and keys and sign as themselves. They are not roles of the node. |
| VTI-KEY-080 – 083 | Attestation artefacts (membership, role and endorsement credentials, vetter grants, status lists, any other credential) are signed by `attestation`. Invitations, removal notices, task documents, DIDComm/TSP signatures and audit checkpoints are signed by `operational`. A general rule covers artefacts not listed. Operational signatures are not evidence of decisions. |
| VTI-KEY-084 – 086 | Registry writes must be operational-signed now. Records SHOULD carry the attestation proof. Until they do, an answer is the registry's assertion, not the node's. |
| VTI-KEY-090 – 094 | `keyRoles` binds each VM to exactly one role. A VM must appear only in the relationship its role requires. Verifiers select by role, never by fragment or position. |
| VTI-KEY-100 – 107 | proofPurpose ↔ relationship check (Data Integrity) and role checks in both directions. In a proof set, a proof under an unsupported cryptosuite is skipped, every checked proof must verify, and at least one must be checked. Hybrid Ed25519 + ML-DSA-44 attestation proofs are allowed. A verifier policy MAY require a named suite (104), and nodes SHOULD publish the suites they sign with so a stripped proof can be detected (105). Operational keys use `authentication`, including on Trust Task documents (106). A proof with no challenge or domain is refused unless the document carries a recipient, a time of issue and an ID, and the verifier applies OPS-023, OPS-024, OPS-026 and OPS-027 to it (107). |
| VTI-KEY-110 – 117 | Custody: attestation and update keys generated non-exportable in the VTA and never in a service backup. Operational keys independent of every other secret. A service-process compromise yields no attestation or log entry except via the VTA oracle. Attestation and update keys are generated, not derived: exempt from KEY-030 and never in any backup, including the VTA's (VTA-050 gains a note). The committed next update key is held in a separate boundary. Recovery from a lost VTA uses that key plus re-issuance (116–117). |
| VTI-KEY-120 – 125 | Planned rotation vs revocation for compromise (with compromise time). Publish-before-use overlap. No overlap on compromise. Pre-rotation mandatory for `update`, deactivate if no sound committed key remains. Retired attestation keys are destroyed. |
| VTI-KEY-130 – 135 | Historical approvals: valid if the key was attestation in the version current at issuance and not compromise-revoked by then. Issuance time comes from the log or a VTA-written status entry, never the artefact's own dates. Re-issuance on compromise. Re-resolution and a 24 h cache cap. Member commit keys: retired means not accepted for new verification, so open changes are re-signed (consistent with KEY-042). |
| VTI-KEY-140 – 148 | 140–145 are withdrawn (the in-place migration is dropped). An identity whose document does not bind key roles is non-conformant (146). Verifiers accept no attestation artefact from it (147). The remedy is a new conformant identity, and the old one is deactivated (148). |
| VTI-KEY-150 – 153 | Privacy: only role IDs and opaque VM ids are published, with no per-relationship keys. Authenticated encryption is preferred over signatures for one-to-one messages. Approver rotation is independent of member events. |
| VTI-VTA-008, 009, 033 | The VTA holds and alone uses attestation/update keys, signs only parsed attestation artefacts with them, and never provisions them in a bundle. |
| VTI-VTC-040 – 043 | The VTC binds roles, never holds attestation/update keys, has companion services sign as themselves, and keeps attestation/update keys out of its backups. |

Also: notes on VTI-OPS-020 and VTI-CRD-002, the terms *key role* and *attestation artefact*, the references [VC-DATA-INTEGRITY] and [FIPS-204], and Security 20–22 and Privacy 14–15.

The rule that a proof's verification method must be in the relationship its proofPurpose names is being proposed separately for the Trust Tasks framework's Proof section. This PR cites that proposal rather than restating it.

### Resolved in review

- The role is renamed `approver` → `attestation`, and the artefacts become *attestation artefacts*, so they are not confused with the APV term *approver*.
- Attestation and update keys are generated, not derived (see KEY-030, VTA-050, KEY-116, KEY-117).
- Operational proofs use `authentication`. The Trust Tasks framework examples, which use `assertionMethod`, need the matching update alongside the proofPurpose↔relationship proposal there.
- Operational requests stay in `authentication`, and `capabilityInvocation` is reserved for a future role.
- There is no migration: existing deployments are test deployments and will be recreated, so the migration requirements are withdrawn and replaced by the non-conformance rule (KEY-146–148).
- Strengthened rather than kept for compatibility:
  - Registry records MUST carry the attestation proof once the protocol can carry it.
  - VM ids MUST NOT reveal a key's role.

### Open issues (marked inline)

1. `keyRoles` needs a JSON-LD term/context. It could live in the DID document, in the webvh parameters, or in a linked resource.
2. There is no capability in Appendix C for attestation-artefact signing.
3. There is no encoding for compromise revocation and compromise time in the webvh log.
4. There is no mechanism yet for a VTA-published issuance record.
5. The 24 h verifier cache cap is a proposal.
6. The registry query protocol has no member for a record's proof.

### Not in this PR

Divergence-register entries for the implementation's current one-key identity templates will follow separately (Appendix F).

`npm run render` completes. The new anchors and terms resolve, and every cited requirement ID is defined.

A VTA or VTC identity today publishes one signing key in both

VTI-KEY-153):

- an extensible registry of key roles -- approver, operational,
  messaging, update -- each fixing what it signs, its verification
  relationship, its proof purpose and its custody (070-077);
- which artefacts are approval artefacts and must be signed by an
  approver key, which are operational, and the registry-record target
  with the transport-level rule for now (080-086);
- a keyRoles property binding each verification method to one role, and
  selection by role rather than fragment (090-094);
- verification: the proofPurpose/relationship rule of Data Integrity,
  role checks, and proof sets in which every evaluated proof must verify
  (100-103);
- custody: approver and update keys generated non-exportable in the VTA,
  never in a service backup; operational secrets independent (110-115);
- per-role rotation and revocation for compromise, overlap, and how an
  approval signed before a rotation is judged, with issuance time never
  taken from the artefact's own dates (120-135);
- migration of legacy identities with a bounded grace period (140-145);
- privacy of what the identifier document reveals (150-153).

The VTA and VTC chapters gain VTI-VTA-008, VTI-VTA-009, VTI-VTA-033 and
VTI-VTC-040 to VTI-VTC-043; operations and credentials gain notes; two
terms, two references and five considerations are added. Existing
requirement text is unchanged. Genuinely open questions are marked
"Open issue" inline.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Rename the approver key role to attestation, and settle four open issues

Applies the review decisions on this proposal.

- The key role `approver` becomes `attestation`, and "approval artefact"
  becomes "attestation artefact", so neither is confused with the
  approver of the Approvals, Consent and Step-Up chapter. The open issue
  on the name is closed.
- Proof sets keep the rule that a proof under an unsupported cryptosuite
  is skipped and every checked proof must verify. A verifier's policy may
  require a named cryptosuite (VTI-KEY-104), and a node should publish the
  suites its attestation artefacts carry so a stripped proof can be seen
  (VTI-KEY-105).
- Attestation and update keys are generated, not derived. They are exempt
  from VTI-KEY-030, never in any backup including the VTA's (VTI-KEY-112),
  and a committed next update key is held in a separate protection
  boundary (VTI-KEY-116). Recovery from a lost VTA relies on the committed
  key and re-issuance (VTI-KEY-117). VTI-KEY-030 carries the exemption and
  VTI-VTA-050 a note.
- Operational keys use the proof purpose `authentication`, on Trust Task
  documents too, with the document's own addressing standing in for
  challenge and domain (VTI-KEY-106). The Trust Tasks framework examples
  are noted as needing the same change.
- Operational requests stay in `authentication`; `capabilityInvocation`
  is reserved for a future registered role.

Stronger where the draft had chosen a weaker option for compatibility:

- a registry record must carry the attestation proof once the query
  protocol can carry it;
- the migration grace period is capped at 90 days, and re-issuance is
  pushed to holders rather than waiting for renewal;
- a VTA must migrate no later than the first node provisioned on it;
- verification method identifiers must not reveal a key's role.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Make an operational proof's replay protection depend on the document checks

VTI-KEY-106 let an authentication proof without challenge or domain stand on the document's own members, conditionally. VTI-KEY-107 makes the dependency unconditional: such a proof is refused unless the document carries a recipient, a time of issue and an identifier, and unless the verifier applies VTI-OPS-023, VTI-OPS-024, VTI-OPS-026 and VTI-OPS-027 to it. Security Considerations item 21 records that the replay protection of operational proofs rests on those requirements.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Replace the key-roles migration with a non-conformance rule

Existing VTA and VTC deployments are test deployments and will be recreated, so no in-place migration is needed. VTI-KEY-140 through VTI-KEY-145 (migration, grace period, re-issue window) are withdrawn and keep their identifiers. VTI-KEY-146 through VTI-KEY-148 state instead that an identity whose document does not bind key roles is non-conformant, that a verifier accepts no attestation artefact from it, and that the remedy is a new conformant identity, the old one being deactivated. The grace-period open issue is closed. Rotation and revocation (VTI-KEY-120 to VTI-KEY-135) are unchanged. The VTA and VTC chapters and Security Considerations item 20 cross-reference the new rule.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: Bound every access control entry by its writer's own, and require full cover to modify one
body:
VTI-ACL-052 forbids a subject to modify its own entry. Nothing stopped the same subject from writing a wider entry for a second identifier it controls. VTI-ACL-042 bounds approve authority and VTI-ACL-071 bounds delegation, but an ordinary grant was bounded on role and context list only. Capabilities, key narrowing and expiry had no bound, so a narrowed context administrator could mint a sibling entry for a DID it holds with none of its own narrowing.

- **VTI-ACL-053 (new).** A caller MUST NOT create or modify an entry, for any subject, that holds authority the caller's own entry does not. This applies on every axis: role, effective capabilities, key narrowing, expiry and approve scope. Additive capabilities stay under VTI-ACL-033. The check is evaluated against the stored entry, not the token, and a caller with no live entry is refused.
- **VTI-ACL-050 (tightened).** Modifying or removing an entry requires the caller's act scope to *cover* the entry's act and approve scopes, not just overlap them. One entry has one capability set, one key filter and one expiry across all its contexts, so an overlapping administrator could change authority in contexts it does not hold. Overlap stays the rule for reading (VTI-ACL-051).
- **VTI-ACL-054 – 058 (new): one-time hand-off.** VTI-ACL-053 also refuses the long-term entry a bootstrap identifier writes for its successor, because that entry outlives its writer.
  - The granter may mark the bootstrap entry at creation. The marker records the granter's authority at that moment.
  - The subject may exercise it exactly once, while the entry is live. The successor is bounded by both the marked entry and the recorded granter authority, and the granter's expiry takes the place of the entry's own.
  - The rollover is atomic, and at most one of concurrent attempts succeeds.
  - It is audited before the commit, and a node that cannot record it does not commit it.
  - No update or rotation can set, extend or carry the marker, and a node MUST NOT infer a hand-off without it.
  - VTI-CLT-017 requires the marker in onboarding flows where the bootstrap identifier writes its own successor.
- **Rationale.** It explains why VTI-ACL-052 and VTI-ACL-053 are each empty without the other. It also explains why the rotation carve-out cannot be abused, since VTI-CLT-029 preserves every axis.

The implementation follows in OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure (linked from there).

`npm run render` completes.

title: security(acl)!: no principal widens its own entry, and no grant exceeds its granter (VTI-ACL-052, VTI-ACL-053)
body:
## Confirmed: self-widening was real, though not on the axes first suspected

Tests written against `main` all fail there, which confirms each case. The test is named in brackets.

Take a context-scoped admin, for example the git bridge's credential (`--role admin --contexts vgi-bridge`). Two widenings were **already refused**: adding a foreign context to its own entry (`require_context`), and raising its role (it is already admin, and `acl/update` requires admin). The following **went through**:

| Path | What went through on `main` | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `acl/update` on own entry | Clearing its own capability narrowing, dropping its own key filter (`allowedKeys: null`), extending its own expiry, relabelling [`vti_acl_052_a_context_admin_cannot_update_its_own_entry`] | VTI-ACL-052 |
| `acl/change-role` on own entry | Accepted [`vti_acl_052_a_subject_cannot_change_its_own_role`] | VTI-ACL-052 |
| `acl/grant` for a second DID it controls | A narrowed admin mints a sibling in the same context with full capabilities, no key filter and no expiry [`vti_acl_053_a_narrowed_admin_cannot_mint_a_wider_sibling`] | VTI-ACL-053 (new, spec PR below) |
| `acl/update` on a peer | Clearing a peer's narrowing past what the caller holds [`vti_acl_053_an_update_cannot_widen_another_entry_past_the_caller`] | VTI-ACL-053 |
| `acl/swap-key` | Dropped `expiresAt`, `allowedKeys`, `approve` and step-up, so a one-hour bootstrap grant became permanent; also reset `createdBy`. This is self-service widening by the subject alone [`vti_clt_029_a_rotation_preserves_the_entry_exactly`] | VTI-CLT-029 |
| `acl/grant` by an initiator | Conferring approve authority it does not hold [`vti_acl_042_an_initiator_cannot_confer_approve_authority_it_lacks`] | VTI-ACL-042 |
| update / change-role / delete | A context-`a` admin changing or removing an entry acting in `[a, b]` [`a_context_admin_cannot_manage_an_entry_reaching_outside_its_contexts`] | VTI-ACL-050 (tightened) |
| any ACL write | By a caller with no ACL entry [`a_caller_without_an_entry_cannot_grant`] | VTI-ACL-001 |

On the VTC:

- `acl/grant` could rewrite the caller's own entry, so re-granting with no `expiresAt` made a time-boxed admin permanent.
- Rewrite, scoped revoke and non-admin role changes needed only overlap.
- **`vtc/admin/invites/create` let any context-scoped admin mint a community-wide (unrestricted) admin entry for any DID, including one it controls.**

## Change

**VTA** (`vta-service/src/operations/acl.rs`, the single choke point every transport reaches):

- REST `routes/acl.rs`, DIDComm `messaging/handlers.rs`, the Trust Task spine `trust_tasks/acl.rs`, and TSP (via the spine) all go through it.
- `refuse_self_modification` on update and change-role. Delete already refused the caller's own entry.
- `validate_within_caller` on create, update and change-role. The resulting entry is measured against the **caller's stored entry**, not its token:
  - Effective capabilities must be a subset of the caller's. Additive `persona-holder` stays under VTI-ACL-033 (super-admin only).
  - The key filter must be a subset of the caller's.
  - The expiry must be no later than the caller's.
  - Approve contexts must be ones the caller can confer in (`acl_entry_can_confer`).
  - A caller with no live entry is refused.
- `caller_covers_entry`: update, change-role and delete require the caller to administer every context the entry acts or approves in.
- update re-runs `validate_role_assignment` and `validate_acl_modification` on the patched entry.
- swap-key clones the entry and changes only the subject. It refuses an expired entry.

**VTC:**

- `routes/acl.rs`: no self-rewrite and no self role change. Coverage is required for every role on rewrite, change-role and revoke. A grant's expiry is bounded by the granter's entry. A granter with no live entry is refused.
- `routes/admin/invites.rs`: an unrestricted admin is required.
- `routes/members/update.rs`: no self role or label change.

**Spec first:** trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#44 adds VTI-ACL-053 (grants are bounded by the granter on every axis) and tightens VTI-ACL-050 from overlap to coverage. VTI-ACL-052, VTI-ACL-042 and VTI-CLT-029 were already normative.

## Breaks (all intended; test instances only, no migration)

- **Onboarding expiry now survives rotation** (VTI-CLT-029). A bootstrap entry granted with `--expires 1h` is still an expiring entry after `acl/swap-key`, and the sweeper removes it when it expires. Grant the bootstrap entry without an expiry, or have an administrator lift it after the swap; the subject cannot lift it.
  - This affects `pnm contexts create --admin-expires`, `vti-secrets` `IntegrationOnboarding`, and any script that relied on the swap discarding the TTL.
  - **Provision-integration rollover by an expiring ephemeral needs the hand-off marker.** Without it the rollover is refused. In the documented flow (`pnm contexts create --admin-did <ephemeral> --admin-expires 1h`), the ephemeral itself is the authenticated caller. Its long-term successor has no expiry, so VTI-ACL-053 refuses it before the ephemeral is retired. The row is kept, but the admin DID minted just before the refusal is left unused. It still works when the ephemeral is granted without an expiry (the rollover retires it), or when an operator whose own entry does not expire runs the provisioning. See **One-time hand-off**.
- A super-admin can no longer relabel its own entry (VTC console, `pnm acl update` on self).
- A narrowed or expiring caller can grant only inside its own bounds. This includes provision-integration run by an operator whose own entry expires.
- An initiator needs approve authority to confer it.
- Entries acting in several contexts are manageable only by an admin covering all of them.
- Context admins cannot send admin invites.
- ACL writes by a DID with no entry are refused. Test fixtures now seed the caller's entry: `TestVtc::token`, `bootstrap_test_vta`, and the VTA ACL unit tests.

## One-time hand-off (VTI-ACL-054 – 058, option (a))

Spec first: trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#44 now also adds VTI-ACL-054 – 058 and VTI-CLT-017.

- **Setting it.** Only the granter can set the marker, and only at creation: `acl/grant` with `ext."org.openvtc.handoff": true`, on every transport.
  - It requires an expiry and a subject other than the caller, and the caller's own entry must carry no marker.
  - It records the granter's role, contexts, capabilities, approve scope, key filter and expiry at that moment.
  - An update naming it is refused. `acl/swap-key` drops it.
- **Using it.** `operations::acl::exercise_handoff`:
  - Only the subject may use it, only while its entry is unexpired, and only once.
  - The successor must fit both the marked entry (its expiry aside) and the recorded granter authority. It takes the granter's expiry.
- **Atomicity and audit.**
  - An `acl.handoff` audit row is written before the commit. If that write fails, nothing is committed.
  - The commit is `KeyspaceHandle::move_if_unchanged`, a new compare-and-move under the keyspace write lock: it writes the successor and removes the marked row only if the row is unchanged since it was validated.
  - A process-wide lock also covers the vsock backend, whose move is not atomic across round-trips.
- **Other admins.** A time-boxed admin without the marker still gets the VTI-ACL-053 refusal (VTI-ACL-058).
- **Provision-integration.** It uses the hand-off when the ephemeral itself rolls over and holds a marker. A lost race is not treated as a harmless retry.
- **Clients.**
  - `pnm contexts create --admin-handoff`, `pnm acl create --handoff`, `cnm contexts create --admin-handoff`, and the offline `vta contexts create --admin-handoff`.
  - SDK: `CreateAclRequest::handoff()` and `AclEntryResponse::handoff()`.
  - The mediator, WebVH and VTC setup hints, and the docs, now include `--admin-handoff`.
  - No migration: rows without the field have no marker.
- **Break.** Onboarding flows that roll over must add `--admin-handoff` to the grant.

## Not changed (reported)

- The token's role and contexts are still snapshots, so a demoted admin keeps its old role in the token until `/auth/refresh`. That is VTI-ACL-080 and a separate issue. The capability, key and expiry bounds here are read live.
- `device/register` still writes `kind` and the device binding onto the caller's own entry. That is metadata, not authority, and it is a spec'd self-service step.
- A context-scoped admin can still create *other* entries up to its own authority in its context. Narrowing a companion service below "context admin" needs the capability discussed on the parent task, not this PR.

## Tests

- `cargo test -p vta-service --lib -- operations::acl`: 45 pass, including 8 new ones that fail on `main`.
- Provision-integration and trust-task tests use the seeded operator.
- `cargo test -p vta-service --test api_integration`: 132 pass. The token helpers now seed the caller's entry.
- `cargo test -p vta-service --lib -- provision_integration`: 65 pass, including the new rollover test.
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --test acl_canonical --test admin_invites`: 27 and 3 pass.
- `unrestricted_admin_consent` (from #1718): a last unrestricted admin's self-demotion is now refused with 403 VTI-ACL-052 instead of reaching the 409 attrition check. The entry is unchanged either way.
- `admin-ui/openapi.json` and `wire.ts` regenerated (invite 403 description).
- New VTC tests:
  - `acl_canonical`: `vti_acl_052_an_admin_cannot_rewrite_its_own_entry`, `vti_acl_052_an_admin_cannot_change_its_own_role`, `vti_acl_053_an_expiring_admin_cannot_grant_past_its_own_expiry`, `a_context_admin_cannot_manage_an_entry_straddling_its_scope`.
  - `admin_invites`: `a_context_scoped_admin_cannot_invite_a_community_wide_admin`.
- Hand-off:
  - `operations::acl`: 51 pass, 6 new. The one rollover succeeds; a second is refused; one after expiry is refused; one widening past the granter is refused; the holder cannot set the marker; a concurrent double rollover yields one success; there is no hand-off without a marker.
  - Swap-key drops the marker.
  - `provision_integration`: 66 pass, including `a_marked_ephemeral_rolls_over_once`.
  - `vti-common` `move_if_unchanged`: 2 pass (16-way race, changed or occupied row).
  - `vta-sdk` `acl_management` and `provision_client`: pass, including the update refusal.

title: Add DTG nodeType property
body:
The [WD02 base structure for DTG credentials](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-cred-spec/#base-structure) still does not include a property identifying the type of DTG node to which a credential is being issued.

This is how all DTG participants can have an unambiguous shared understanding of the types of nodes with which they have relationships — and apply policy against this metadata (canonical example: applying [proof of personhood](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.07892) policies to a `person`).

Proposal: in WD03 (aka WD 0.3.0) under the `CredentialSubject` property, add a subproperty following the `id` property

- `nodeType` (string, REQUIRED): MUST include exactly one of `"person"`, `"device"`, `"agent"`, `"VTC"`, or `"VTN"`.

title: Decide the home of the DTG namespace before the Implementers Draft
body:
## Summary

#47 makes VSC predicates absolute IRIs on the wire, so the core predicates are now written out in full. The PR writes them under the existing context URL plus `#`:

```
https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1#endorses
https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1#witnessed
```

That is a default inherited from the `@context` requirement in Base Structure, not a decision anyone has made. The namespace is where every predicate this WG defines will live, it is the prefix communities will copy when they define their own vocabularies, and it is what the planned DTG Predicate Vocabulary specification will be published under. It needs an owner.

## Why it has to be decided early

Changing the namespace later is a find-and-replace in the spec but a migration for every credential issued under it: a predicate IRI is compared byte-exact (Predicate Handling in #47), so a credential issued under the old namespace does not match a verifier configured for the new one. That cost is zero today and grows with every issued credential. **This should be settled as soon as possible, and at the latest before the specification bumps to an Implementers Draft**, since that is the point at which implementations start issuing credentials that have to keep verifying.

The same question applies to the `@context` IRI itself, which Base Structure already requires and which is not yet published either; the two should be decided together.

## Options

1. **Keep `https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1#`.** No change to the spec. The vocabulary — and the context — are then hosted and controlled by First Person, and the DTG Predicate Vocabulary spec, if it becomes a ToIP deliverable, would define terms under a namespace ToIP does not control.
2. **Move to a ToIP-controlled IRI.** For example under `https://trustoverip.org/...` or another origin the Foundation administers. The context and vocabulary are then governed with the specification. Requires ToIP to agree to host and maintain the resources, and a find-and-replace in the spec before any credential is issued.

## What the decision needs to cover

- The namespace IRI for DTG-defined predicates.
- The `@context` IRI (currently `https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1`), and whether the namespace is that URL plus `#` or a separate IRI.
- Who administers the origin, and the commitment that published context and vocabulary versions are immutable (a requirement in #47).
- Versioning: whether `v1` in the path is the context version, the vocabulary version, or both.

## Proposed resolution

Decide at the next editors' call, record the answer here, and apply it to #47 before merge or in a follow-up PR before the Implementers Draft.

Refs #45, #47.
author: geoffturk

title: Carry the trust-task citation in committed form: taskContext and taskDigestMultibase are durable correlators (ZKP record 008)
body:
**What is asked.** A credential that cites the exchange it was issued in carries the citation in the clear: under [PR #56](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/56), `taskContext` (the initiating document's `id`) and `taskDigestMultibase` (its task digest). Both are stable across every presentation of that credential, so a credential presented twice is linked by its citation even where everything else about it is proven in zero knowledge. The ZKP specification's [record 008](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-zkp-spec/#construction-008-blinded-binder-taskcontext-hiding-presentation-correlation-unresolved) (blinded binder) asks the credential layer for one member: a committed form of the citation that a holder can open, in proof, to the exchange a verifier already holds.

**The shape.** Route 1 of record 008: the issuer carries `C = commit(taskContext, taskDigestMultibase; u)` with a blinding value `u` the holder keeps; a verifier that holds the exchange checks the opening, or in a proof the holder shows that `C` opens to the exchange the verifier names. Route 2 — a per-context pseudonym derived by a PRF from the holder secret and a context descriptor — is the fuller construction and stays on the ZKP side. The record also states what neither route gives: a visible `C` still links presentations of the same credential; hiding `C` inside the proof is what removes that.

**What is this specification's to decide**, so the Credentials TF can schedule it:

- whether the committed form replaces the pair or sits beside it under a profile;
- the member name(s), and that the value is `digestMultibase`-encoded per §Digest Encoding so both layers agree on the encoding;
- generation, distribution and retention of `u` — never published beside a low-entropy plaintext;
- how §Outcome Interpretability pairs a committed citation with outcome evidence: the verifier that holds the outcome evidence already holds the plaintext, so the opening is against what it holds, and nothing is lost there.

**What stays with the ZKP TF:** the proof that `C` opens to the exchange, its composition into the enclosing records, the per-context pseudonym — record 008 on `main`, re-read against PR #56 in [dtgwg-zkp-spec PR #11](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-zkp-spec/pull/11).

**Relation to #38.** `taskDigestMultibase` is a digest over a document, so the enumeration concern of #38 reaches it; record 022 (PR #11) covers the digest-valued members and would cover this one on the same terms. This issue is the citation's committed form, not its salt.

Filed at the credential maintainer's request on the ZKP working draft review (16 September). [PR #18](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/18) is parked and is not this issue.

⚔️⊥⿻⊥🧙

title: Name the property and @context term that carry a correlation-scope declaration
body:
## Summary

WD02 says every identifier has a declared [correlation scope](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/blob/main/spec/body.md#correlation-scope) of `pairwise`, `directed` or `public`, and §Declaring scope settles *where* the declaration lives: in the credential, made by the issuer about its own identifier. What it does not settle is the property that carries it or the `@context` term for that property. The editor's note at the end of the subsection records that:

> The property that carries the declaration, and its `@context` term, are not yet named. Until they are, the requirements of this section bind a declaration that has been made and do not require one; the examples in this specification carry no declaration.

This issue tracks naming it. The decision was taken in #30's rebase (review item 4) and recorded in the #31 merge plan; neither is a place anyone will look once #31 closes.

## Why it matters

- **The section is normative in form and void in practice.** The reuse check, the ordering rule and the verifier rules all key off a declared value, and no conforming credential can carry one. An implementation today cannot declare a scope and cannot be non-conforming for failing to.
- **The examples are silent.** Every example in the specification omits the declaration, so none demonstrates the mechanism the section defines. The readability note in the introduction already says the reused member identifier is `directed`; once the property exists the examples should say so themselves.
- **Downstream text assumes it exists.** The witness `directed` minimum, the VDC delegator guidance (Privacy Consideration 10), the VMC acknowledgement item, and the common-control discussion in #9 all reason about declared scopes as if a verifier can read them.

## What has to be decided

1. **The property name**, and whether it sits at the top level of the credential or inside a structure alongside the issuer identifier. The declaration is a property of the identifier rather than of the credential (§Declaring scope, first consequence), which argues for a placement that reads that way.
2. **The `@context` term** under `https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1`.
3. **Whether the reciprocal credential in a bidirectional edge may restate the counterparty's scope** for readability, or whether each half carries only its issuer's own declaration, as the second consequence in §Declaring scope currently implies.
4. **Populate the examples** with computed declarations, and delete the editor's note.

Placement in the DID document is already ruled out and should not be reopened: `did:key` and `did:peer` numalgo-0 documents are derived from the identifier value, and those are the methods the specification recommends for the two narrow scopes.

## Migration note carried over from #30

#30's description records that Keyring Wallet fixtures (`ref-07-dtg-edge-semantics`) were built against the earlier four-value draft of #22 and declare `community`, a value that does not map onto one scope; each has to be re-decided as `pairwise` or `directed` per fixture. `rDid` is also a DIDComm wire field in the VRC reference implementation, so retiring it is a peer-compatibility change. #31 asked that the fixture owner be told before WD02 was cut. WD02 has since been cut (#44) and nothing records the outcome. Since the property named here is what those fixtures will declare, this is the natural place to confirm the fixtures have been re-decided, or to record that they have not.

title: Digest-valued binders are unsalted and enumerable; blinding is deferred from WD02
body:
## Summary

Every digest-valued binder in this specification — the VWC `digestMultibase`, the member-issued VMC `digestMultibase` (#12), and the VDC `delegation.parent` / `delegation.accepts` (#19) — is an unsalted JCS-SHA-256 digest over content that is often low-entropy. Where a verifier is shown the digest but not the referenced credential, an observer who knows the schema and the governing vocabulary can recover the referenced content by enumeration.

## Where this was raised

@stormer78's design note in [dtgwg-cred-tf#40](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf/discussions/40), edge case E3: a VTC publishes forty scope strings; a commitment to a `scope` array is matched by enumerating plausible subsets in milliseconds. The same shape applies to a VWC digest over a VRC whose two identifiers are known, and to a VMC acknowledgement digest over a grant whose fields are predictable. The ZKP task force took this as a work item ([dtgwg-cred-tf#39](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-tf/discussions/39), ScottJeezey, 25 August): salted commitments available now, PRF-derived per-context pseudonyms as the fuller construction.

## Why it is not in WD02

It is cross-cutting — it changes the hashed representation of three credential types at once — and the construction (a salt member in the hashed block, ACDC-style `u`; a SAID; or a ZK commitment) is a choice the ZKP task force is working through. #19 lands the encoding (Multibase/Multihash per VC Data Integrity §2.6, per #17) without changing what is hashed, so a blinding scheme can be added to the canonicalization step later without a second encoding migration.

## What this issue tracks

- Whether WD03 should add a salt to the hashed representation of every digest-valued binder, and where it lives.
- Whether the same construction serves the anchoring / revocation-status / registry-membership unification proposed in cred-tf#40 §5.
- Coordination with the ZKP task force's Q2 (blinded binder) work.

Related: #9 (common-control linkage, the other cross-TF dependency).

title: feat(pnm): up to ~20× faster commands on a distant VTA (ssh-style ControlMaster)
body:
> **Draft / WIP** — the feature works and is measured, but see *Not done yet* at the bottom.

## Why

Every `pnm` invocation is a fresh process. Each one re-resolves the VTA and mediator DIDs,
opens a TLS connection per host, authenticates to the mediator and upgrades a WebSocket —
and only then sends the command. None of that survives the process, so the next command
pays for all of it again.

On a local stack that is invisible: a round trip costs microseconds, so the setup is free
and every command looks instant. Against a VTA in another region it is the whole story.

Counted off the reverse proxy's access log, one `pnm acl list` over DIDComm is **12–17 HTTPS
requests**: 6 `did.jsonl` fetches, a mediator challenge and authenticate, a WebSocket
upgrade, an inbox drain, the actual outbound/inbound pair, and several cleanup `DELETE`s.
Because each fresh connection also pays TCP and TLS on top of its request, that is **~23
serialised round trips** — for a command whose useful work is one.

## What it costs today, and with this change

`pnm acl list`, three runs per cell, median. Both arms are the same binary and the same
`docker exec` into one long-lived container, so process startup is in neither number; the
~103 ms exec floor is subtracted. Latency injected with a delaying relay in front of the
stack, so these are propagation delay only — no jitter or loss, which makes them floors.

| RTT | one-shot (`--control-master no`) | multiplexed | removed | **ratio** |
|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| 0 ms | 64 ms | 41 ms | 23 ms | **1.6×** |
| 50 ms | 1 378 ms | 107 ms | 1 271 ms | **12.9×** |
| 150 ms | 3 646 ms | 215 ms | 3 431 ms | **17.0×** |
| 300 ms | 6 892 ms | 360 ms | 6 532 ms | **19.1×** |

Both sides are linear in RTT, which is the useful form:

```
one-shot     ≈ 22.8 × RTT
multiplexed  ≈  1.06 × RTT
```

The ratio therefore climbs with distance and approaches **~21×** (22.8 / 1.06) as the
fixed local cost stops mattering: 19.1× is what was measured at 300 ms, not a ceiling.

A multiplexed command costs **one application round trip** — the same thing a trust ping
measures. So the rule needs no RTT estimate at all: **the multiplexed number is your trust
ping**, and everything above it is setup the one-shot CLI redoes every time.

| your trust ping | multiplexed | one-shot today |
|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| 50 ms | 50 ms | ~1.2 s |
| 150 ms | 150 ms | ~3.5 s |
| 300 ms | 300 ms | ~7.0 s |

At 300 ms RTT a twenty-command script goes from over two minutes to about seven seconds.

### Starting the master is ~free

The first command has no master to talk to, so it starts one and then delegates. That costs
about what running the command directly would have, because the master does the setup the
command needed anyway:

| RTT | first command (starts master) | one-shot |
|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| 0 ms | 168 ms | 64 ms |
| 50 ms | 1 432 ms | 1 378 ms |
| 150 ms | 3 638 ms | 3 646 ms |
| 300 ms | 7 044 ms | 6 892 ms |

Which is why the default can be `auto`: nobody has to think about it, and nobody pays to
find out.

## What this adds

```
--control-master no|auto|yes|ask    (default: auto)
--control-persist no|yes|10m|600    (default: 10m)
--control-path <PATH>               (default: per-VTA socket in a private dir)

pnm sidecar serve | status | stop   (ssh -M / -O check / -O exit)
```

Names and semantics follow `ssh_config(5)` so the behaviour transfers. Rarely typed:
`auto` starts a master on demand, the way nobody types `ssh -M`.

The client hands the master its own stdin/stdout/stderr over `SCM_RIGHTS`, so a delegated
command's output is indistinguishable from a direct one — same terminal, same `isatty`,
same colours, same redirection.

## Why it is safe to default on

A master that is missing, stale, wrong-version or unusable is **never an error**. Every
such path falls back to the ordinary one-shot command, so the worst case is exactly
today's behaviour. Verified by killing a master with `SIGKILL` and running the next
command: the stale socket is detected, unlinked, replaced, and the command succeeds.

## Security

The master holds the only copy of the operator's admin private key in memory and will run
any command handed to it, so the socket is the privilege boundary:

- control directory forced to `0700` and ownership-checked; socket `0600`
- a symlinked or foreign-owned control path is refused, which closes the path-swap race
- **peer uid verified on every connection** (`SO_PEERCRED` / `getpeereid`) rather than
  trusting file permissions alone, with no exemption for root
- protocol version checked, so a master left running across an upgrade is refused rather
  than guessed at
- `--control-persist 10m` bounds how long the key stays resident — a security control, not
  just resource hygiene
- `ask` confirms before a master is used or created

## Two details taken from the OpenSSH implementation, not its documentation

1. **The socket is claimed atomically.** Binding a temp path and `link()`ing it into place
   means a second master loses with `EEXIST`. The obvious `unlink()`-then-`bind()` would
   remove a live master's socket, leaving that master running but unreachable while every
   later client silently started another. There is a regression test for this.
2. **Stale sockets are removed by the client, on `ECONNREFUSED` only**, and not at all when
   multiplexing is disabled.

Deliberate divergences from ssh are documented in `control/client.rs`: we spawn a child
rather than forking a thread-bearing tokio process; we confirm on the client's terminal so
`ask` works headless (ssh's askpass silently denies with no `DISPLAY`); we vet the control
path, which ssh does not; we do not exempt root from the peer check; and `yes` means "never
silently fall back" rather than ssh's "be the master".

No OpenSSH code is used — the design is reimplemented in Rust.

## Testing

`cargo test -p pnm-cli` — 104 pass, including the socket race, socket mode, path
sanitisation, symlink refusal and the `ControlPersist` time vocabulary. `clippy` and `fmt`
clean.

Against a live stack: idle timeout evicts the master, `sidecar stop` exits it, a
`SIGKILL`ed master is recovered from, `--control-master no` still runs direct, and the
control socket is `0600` inside a `0700` directory on both macOS and Linux.

## Not done yet

- [ ] `-O stop` (stop-listening) as distinct from `-O exit` — matters less here, where a
      session is one short command rather than a shell
- [ ] config-file keys to match the flags, so a default can be set per VTA
- [ ] review of whether `auto` should be the shipped default or opt-in for a release or two
- [ ] the `ask` prompt is per master, not per command — worth deciding which is wanted

title: feat(vtc): step-up passkeys a member enrols through an admin's invite
body:
Stacked on #1745 (base `feat/git-ns-break-glass`). Implements the step-up credential specified in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#645.

## Why

A git break-glass always needs a passkey gesture bound to that one request (`acl::bound_step_up`). A namespace admin who is not a console user acts only through signed documents, so the community knows no passkey of theirs and they could never break the glass. Their signing key alone must not be able to enrol one, or a stolen key would enrol the thief's passkey. So the first step-up passkey is anchored in a community administrator's single-use invite, redeemed with a claim code sent over a different channel.

## What

- **`step_up_passkey`**
  - `auth/passkey/enroll/invite/0.2` with `purpose: stepUp`.
  - `auth/passkey/enroll/redeem/{start,finish}/0.1`.
  - `auth/passkey/revoke/{start,finish}/0.2`, for an administrator revoking on the member's behalf.
- **Invite rules**
  - Only a community admin can issue one, from a stepped-up session, and never to themselves.
  - The subject must be a current member.
  - The claim code is Argon2id-hashed and shown once. It is never in the URL, and the token travels in the fragment (`/admin/enrol-step-up#token=…`).
  - Each invite is single use. Five wrong codes void it.
  - A wrong token and a wrong code get the same refusal.
  - A second step-up passkey needs a user-verified gesture from the first.
  - The redeem routes are on the governed unauthenticated chain.
- **Step-up only, by construction**
  - The credentials live in their own keyspace, `step_up_passkeys`, which login and session step-up never read.
  - `acl::bound_step_up` offers them alongside the actor's session passkeys, and accepts them only for the actor's own step-up.
  - A revoked one loses its mapping, so it cannot answer a step-up that was already pending.
- **Audit**: `AuditEvent::StepUpPasskeyChanged`, with stages `invited`, `registered`, `inviteInvalidated` and `revoked`. The token and the code are never recorded.
- **Backup**: excluded, like `passkey`.
- **Console**
  - A *Step-up passkeys* card on the member page. Invite shows the link and the claim code separately. Revoke verifies with the admin's own passkey.
  - A sign-in-free `/admin/enrol-step-up` page.
  - `/admin/step-up` opens standalone without a session and answers unsigned when the browser holds no console key. The WebAuthn assertion is the gate.
- **cnm**: the step-up prompt now names the step-up passkey.
- **Docs**: `docs/03-vtc/git-namespaces.md` (*Step-up passkeys for members*), `backup-restore.md`, and `CLAUDE.md`.

## Tests

- New `vtc-service/tests/step_up_passkeys.rs` drives the whole flow with the soft authenticator:
  - invite, redeem, then a bound step-up answered by an **unsigned** approve-response and spent once;
  - the credential never appears in the session store;
  - wrong-code counting and voiding;
  - single use, and the second-passkey gesture;
  - admin-only invites and no self-invites;
  - a revoked passkey cannot answer a pending step-up.
- Also passing: `signed_step_up`, `openapi_snapshot`, `openapi_response_census`, `trust_task_manifest`, `vti-common` audit, and `vtc-service` lib `store::keyspaces`, `acl::bound_step_up` and `routes::openapi`. Clippy is clean on `vtc-service`, `vti-common` and `cnm-cli`.
- Console: `tsc`, `wire:check`, and 464 vitest tests (new `step-up-passkeys.test.ts`, plus an unsigned-answer case in `bound-step-up.test.ts`).

These tests were run locally against a trust-tasks-rs built from #641 plus #645.

## Needs

A trust-tasks-rs release that carries trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#645 as well as #641. Until then this compiles only with `--config 'patch.crates-io.trust-tasks-rs.path=…'`, and CI will fail to resolve the new modules.

## Not in this PR

- A member revoking their own step-up passkey. `revoke/start` 0.2 allows it, but it needs a signed document plus a browser ceremony. Today an administrator revokes on the member's behalf.
- Telling the member over DIDComm when a credential is bound or revoked. The specs make this a SHOULD.

title: fix(vtc-service)!: a community backup travels only over DIDComm or TSP
body:
## Summary

A community backup now travels only over a channel confidential end-to-end: DIDComm or TSP. It is never sent over REST or HTTPS.

The backup request carries its password, and the backup itself carries the community's signing key bundle. Over REST, both exist in plaintext wherever TLS terminates. Whoever holds that point could sign as the community.

The VTA side of the same change is #1733. The spec is trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#646. It covers `vtc/backup/{export,import}` 0.1 and the node-neutral `backup/*` 0.1 family.

## Changes

### VTC

- **Bearer routes:** `POST /v1/backup/export` and `POST /v1/backup/import` always answer 403, and the message names the fix. Their request-body types are removed.
- **Trust Tasks:** these tasks are refused on the REST binding with `permissionDenied`:
  - `vtc/backup/export/0.1`
  - `backup/initiate-export/0.1`
  - `backup/initiate-import/0.1`
  - `backup/finalize-import/0.1`

  The check runs after the super-admin check, and before any state is serialized, a slot is opened or the password is used. `get-chunk`, `put-chunk`, `complete-export` and `abort` carry only ciphertext or handles, so they are unaffected.
- **Authority:** unchanged. Every verb still requires an unrestricted administrator, read from the signer's ACL row. The VTC's ACL has no capability narrowing, so super-admin is its equivalent of the VTA's `key-export`.
- **Audit before release:** `export_inner` already wrote the `BackupExported` row before returning the envelope, and refused the export if the write failed. It now also refuses when the VTC has no audit trail at all. Before, it released the backup unrecorded. This covers `vtc/backup/export` and `backup/initiate-export`.

### vtc-client

- `export_backup` runs `backup/initiate-export`, then `get-chunk` for every chunk, then `complete-export`, over the client's DIDComm or TSP session. It checks every chunk against the manifest, and the whole against the committed SHA-256 and size.
- `import_backup` runs `initiate-import`, then `put-chunk` for every chunk, then `finalize-import`, which carries the password. A committed import now reports `status: committed`.
- Both refuse without a session (`VtcError::Session`), before anything is sent.
- New dependencies: `sha2` and `base64` (workspace).

### cnm

- `cnm backup export` and `cnm backup import` connect with `vtc::connect_end_to_end`. It uses TSP when the VTC advertises it, falls back to DIDComm if TSP fails, and uses DIDComm when TSP is not advertised. There is no REST fallback.
- `cnm` now builds `vtc-client` with `tsp`, which includes `didcomm`.

### Docs

- `docs/03-vtc/backup-restore.md` now describes the channel rule and the chunked transfer. The curl examples are removed.

## Breaking changes

- `POST /v1/backup/{export,import}` always answer 403.
- The backup Trust Tasks are refused over `POST /v1/trust-tasks`.
- `cnm backup` needs a VTC that advertises DIDComm or TSP.
- A VTC with no audit trail cannot export.
- `vtc-client::import_backup` returns the `finalize-import` reply, whose commit status is `committed` rather than `imported`.

## Tests

- `an_export_over_rest_is_refused`
- `an_export_with_no_audit_trail_is_refused`
- `the_password_bearing_verbs_are_refused_over_rest` (`backup/*`)
- `backup_export_and_import_are_refused_over_rest` (bearer routes, integration)
- `a_backup_needs_a_session`
- `backup_chunks_encode_and_digest_consistently` (vtc-client)
- The existing `backup/*` round-trip and `vtc/backup/export` tests now run over DIDComm.
- The bearer-route error-code tests are removed. Their codes are covered on the Trust Task door.

title: feat(cli)!: make pnm usable from a script
body:
## Why

A script cannot trust what `pnm` reports.

- `--json` accepted and ignored on seven commands. Exit 0, human text. The parse error lands in a later stage, nowhere near the cause.
- `pnm health` printed a cross and exited 0, so a pipeline stayed green over a dead mediator. A profile with no VTA configured also exited 0, having checked nothing.
- `PNM_HOME` accepted and ignored. An operation believed sandboxed ran against the real profile.
- Every error exited 1. A missing name, a bad argument and an expired credential were indistinguishable.
- Colour and a six-line logo went into pipes and logs.
- `acl create --help` pointed at a command that refuses the job.

## What

Terminal gets the table, colour and banner. Anything else gets json. `--json` still forces json on a terminal. `NO_COLOR` honoured.

Exit codes: 1 failed, 2 usage, 3 not found, 4 config, 5 auth. Picked from the SDK's typed error in the one place every command lands, so a call site does not have to know one. Being refused a permission stays 1: the operation ran and failed, which is not the same signal as a bad credential.

`health` derives its exit status from its checks and emits one document per check. A run that checked nothing is not a pass.

`PNM_HOME` moves config, sessions, pending setups and bootstrap secrets together.

## Breaking

Piped output is json. Scripts parsing the human table must read json instead.

Human output at a terminal is byte-identical to before: same banner, colours and tables.

## Not covered

Backup password on stdin, re-point after a VTA rebuild, `--outcome` matching, `--full-display` truncation, and guarding an unreissuable admin credential, which needs provenance nothing persists today.

title: fix!: verify every VTA reply, and sign the TSP announce
body:
This is the app side of OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1744. It follows two VTI changes:

- #1739: the VTA and the VTC accept a Trust Task over DIDComm or TSP only when its proof verifies as its `issuer`, and that issuer is the transport sender.
- #1740: every VTA and VTC response, errors included, is signed under `proofPurpose: authentication`.

## What the app sends

The app already sent only signed documents built by the engine: `whoami`, step-up approve/deny, task-consent approve/deny and `device/set-wake`, each with a fresh `urn:uuid` id, `issuedAt`, `issuer` set to the device `did:key` and `recipient` set to the VTA. With #1744 the engine:

- signs these under `authentication`, except the approver's own decisions: the step-up `approve-response` and the `task-consent/decision` (approve and deny for each). These are evidence the executor records, so they are signed under `assertionMethod`, and only with a key the device's `did:key` lists there;
- refuses to send any document that is unsigned, or is not issued by this holder to this VTA.

The one unsigned document was the TSP reachability announce, an unsigned `messaging/ping/0.1` that #1739 refuses. It is replaced by `VtaMobileAgent.announceTsp`, which sends a holder-signed ping. The engine's `announce` is removed.

The app sends none of the legacy DIDComm protocol messages that #1739 removes. It uses only the Trust Task envelope over DIDComm and the TSP binding envelope.

## Pushed approval requests

The step-up approve-request, consent request and task-consent request the VTA pushes are its operational messages. #1740 signs them with the operational key under `authentication`, and the #1744 engine refuses one signed under `assertionMethod`, or with a key the issuer does not list under `authentication`, before it prompts. The signed step-up fixtures in `AuthorizationContextTests` are re-signed under `authentication` with the same deterministic test key (seed 17). They were re-signed and checked with the engine's `verify_signed_request` in a throwaway Rust test.

## How replies are verified

| Transport | Where | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| DIDComm | engine, inside `MediatorSession.sendTrustTask` | proof by the VTA under `authentication` (key listed under `authentication`); `threadId` and `type` answer the request; issued by the VTA to this device |
| TSP | `TspReplyRouter.deliver`, via `verifyTrustTaskReply` | same, checked **before** the waiting `submit` is resolved |

Over TSP, a frame that echoes a `threadId` but fails verification is not consumed. The expectation stays open, so the genuine reply still resolves the submit, and a reply that never verifies times out. Error replies must verify too.

## Also

- Re-vendors `Sources/VtaMobileCore/VtaMobileCore.swift`, generated from the #1744 engine. The diff is large because the generator on main has moved on since the v0.6.17 release was vendored.
- The `Package.swift` pin TODO now points at #1744. Until a `vta-mobile-core-v*` release is cut from #1744 and the tag and checksum here are bumped, a checkout needs the local-xcframework override. **CI on this PR is expected to fail until then**: the v0.6.17 binary does not match the vendored bindings, and it still expects pushed requests under `assertionMethod`. No release is cut as part of this PR.
- The README and doc comments describe proof-bound requests and verified replies instead of intrinsic-sender auth, and the exception for the approver's decisions.

## Verification

No full Xcode is installed on the machine this was prepared on (Command Line Tools only), so `xcodebuild test` on a simulator and the XCTest suite were **not** run. What was run:

- `swiftc -typecheck` of `Sources/VtaMobileCore` and `Sources/VtaMobileAgent` against the regenerated bindings and FFI header (macOS target): clean.
- `App/` type-checked for Mac Catalyst (`arm64-apple-ios16.0-macabi`): clean apart from the `#Preview` macro, whose plugin ships only with Xcode.
- A throwaway macOS executable linking the host build of the #1744 engine, exercising the router and the real verifier. All checks passed:
  - a forged reply is not consumed, and the genuine reply resolves the waiter;
  - an unexpected thread passes through;
  - a reply that never verifies times out;
  - the engine refuses an unsigned reply with `UnverifiedReply`;
  - the default router does not consume an unsigned reply.
- The updated `TspReplyRouterTests`, including three new cases for these rules, and the re-signed `AuthorizationContextTests` fixtures were written but not compiled, since XCTest is unavailable here (`swiftc -parse` only).

Not run: an end-to-end test against a deployed VTA built from #1739 and #1740.
