title: feat(vtc/vetting/vetters/event-mode): the exception to the constant drip (#620)
body:
feat(vtc/vetting/vetters/event-mode): the exception to the constant drip (#620)

A vetter's ordinary rate is a few tokens a tick, whether or not they have
vetted anyone. That is the right rate for ordinary weeks and the wrong one for
a conference desk, and the answer is deliberately not a bigger drip under the
same key: it is a separate token label for a named event, with its own rate,
its own expiry, and a group of vetters large enough that a spend under it still
hides one.

This task carries the vetter's half of that, which is only ever a request. The
approval is an act by someone else, through the community's own administrative
surface, and the specification says why there is no Trust Task for it: a task
the vetter could send is a task a vetter could be made to send.

The response says where the request stands, and carries a group *count* rather
than a group. Who else is at the event is the anonymity set, so the number is
the most a member may be told — enough to tell "nobody has approved it" from
"not enough people have asked", which are the two reasons a request waits.

title: fix(vtc): carry the applicant's registryConsent onto the admitted member
body:
## Keyring round 3, Q14: `registryConsent` does nothing

Keyring (Berkman Center's Keyring wallet team) asked what `registryConsent` on `vtc/join-requests/submit` actually does (round-3 question **Q14**, no VTI-nn number; tracked in `design-docs/keyring-round3-plan.md`). The answer was: nothing.

### Root cause

`registryConsent` is the applicant's opt-in to trust-registry publication. The spec says so: `specs/vtc/join-requests/submit/0.2/spec.md` § Security & Privacy → *Consent/purpose*, plus the payload schema description ("Whether the applicant consents to trust-registry publication"). The VTC stored it on the `JoinRequest` row (`join/orchestrate.rs` `realize_join_verdict`), and nothing read it after that. Admission built the member with `Member::fresh`, which hard-codes `publish_consent: false` (`members/mod.rs`), on every path. So the applicant's answer never reached the member, and the only way a member's `publish_consent` ever became `true` was an admin `members/update`.

### What changed

- `EffectPlan::Admit` gains `publish_consent: bool`, and the admit executor writes it onto the Member row in its **first** store, under the existing `LAST_ADMIN_LOCK`. No second write, and no moment where the row exists without it.
- It is set from the join request on every path that admits one:
  - **auto-admit on submit** and **a supplement that admits**. Both go through the shared `apply_verdict_to_request` (#1593), which now reads `request.registry_consent` off the row it decides. Invitation redemption is a submit carrying `consume_invitation_id`, so it takes this path too.
  - **operator approval of a referred (`pending`) request** (`routes/join_requests/decide.rs` `approve_pending`), set from `req.registry_consent`. An approval admits the applicant. It does not consent on the applicant's behalf.
- `ceremony::plan` (verdict → plan, with no join request in hand) always writes `false`, because a verdict cannot consent for anyone.
- If the field is absent or `false`, the result is `false`, the same as before.
- Doc comments updated. `openapi.json` and `wire.ts` were regenerated (the only change is the `registryConsent` description).

### Re-admission / admin changes (decision)

Admission can never overwrite a **live** member's consent. A live member holds an ACL row, so `admit` returns `Conflict` before touching the Member row. That means a later admin `members/update` of `publish_consent` survives for the life of the membership. Re-admission only happens after a departure, and the tombstone already clears `publish_consent`. The new application's `registryConsent` is the only answer that applies to the new membership, so it is written as-is. A departed member's old consent does not carry into a new membership. There is no renewal path that re-runs admission.

### What the opt-in now does, and what still doesn't (honest scope)

After this change, `publish_consent` shows the applicant's own answer: in `members/read`, on the admin console's member panel ("Publish consent"), and to anything that consults it later.

**Nothing enforces it yet.** The registry syncer (`registry/tail.rs` → `syncer.rs`) turns every `MemberAdded` into a `PublishMember` job, gated only by `registry.rego`'s `publish_on_join` (default `true`). **It never reads `publish_consent`.** So when a registry is configured, members are published whether or not they consented. Before this PR, `false` was stored for everyone and ignored. Now the applicant's real answer is stored, and it is still ignored. Gating `PublishMember` / `UpdateMember` on `publish_consent` (and deciding what an admin flipping it later should trigger: publish or delete) is the follow-up. I left it out of this PR because it changes default registry behaviour: with the default `false`, nobody gets published unless they opt in, and that deserves its own review.

**Spec follow-up (not opened):** the spec says what `registryConsent` grants (trust-registry publication and nothing else, and a consumer MUST NOT read `true` as agreement to anything more). It does **not** say that a consumer MUST NOT publish without it, or that the answer binds the resulting membership. A clarification PR to `trust-tasks-tf` is a follow-up.

### Tests

New in `vtc-service/tests/join_requests.rs`:
- `auto_admit_carries_registry_consent_onto_the_member`: `true` → `true`, `false` → `false`, absent → `false`
- `an_approved_referral_carries_registry_consent_onto_the_member`: submitted as pending, then an operator approves; covers both `true` and `false`
- `a_supplement_that_admits_carries_registry_consent_onto_the_member`: deferred request with consent, supplemented under an allow policy

Run:
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast` (default features include `tsp`): all green
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo fmt --all`
- `UPDATE_OPENAPI=1 cargo test --test openapi_snapshot`, then `npm run wire:generate` / `wire:check`

### Checklist
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): consent is written inside the existing admit lock, and no network happens under it
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): n/a
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*): no wire shape change, only an internal enum field; the OpenAPI description text and wire.ts were regenerated
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*): absent `registryConsent` → `false`
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*): the `Member::publish_consent` doc now says the syncer does not enforce it
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): consent is part of the first Member write, not a follow-up patch
- [x] Deviations flagged: none

title: feat(vtc): the admin member tasks are served as signed documents
body:
Refs #1641 — phase 2, batch 1.

The VTC's admin-facing member verbs declare `proof` REQUIRED and were served
only as flat-payload REST behind a bearer JWT, so they got none of what the
dispatcher enforces: no proof, no recipient binding, no acceptance window, and
nothing in the accepted-id record. This binds the first four in the document
dispatcher, where all of that applies.

## What moved

| Task | REST route | signed door |
|---|---|---|
| `vtc/members/credentials/0.1` | `GET /v1/members/{did}/credentials` | `POST /v1/trust-tasks` (+ DIDComm, TSP) |
| `vtc/members/update/0.1` | `PATCH /v1/members/{did}` | same |
| `vtc/members/admin-remove/0.1` | `DELETE /v1/members/{did}` | same |
| `vtc/members/purge/0.1` | `DELETE /v1/members/{did}/purge` | same |

The set was re-derived from `routes/mod.rs`'s `tt()` bindings against each
spec's front matter in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf: all four declare
`proofRequirement: REQUIRED` and `issuedAtRequirement: REQUIRED`, and all four
have a generated `Payload`/`Response` pair, which is what the arms emit. Nothing
was dropped — `members/update` was kept despite #1645 having reshaped it,
because its `adminRoleForbidden` refusal fires before anything is read and is
exactly what makes the one session-dependent path (promotion) unreachable.

Each verb's route body was lifted into a transport-free inner
(`read_member_credentials`, `update_member_inner`, `admin_remove_inner`;
`purge_member` already was one) that both doors call, so the two cannot answer
differently.

## Authorization: the signer's ACL entry, not a bearer token

`admin_signer` takes the DID the spine verified the proof against — bound to the
document's own `issuer` per SPEC §4.7 — and reads its authority from
`crate::acl::resolve_auth_role` **at execution time**.

Every check the bearer extractors made is still made:

- `AdminAuth` ⇒ `VtcRole::Admin`. `resolve_auth_role` admits only that row and
  answers `Forbidden` for absent, expired, or non-admin — which is where the
  JWT's `role` claim came from in the first place (`map_vtc_role_to_auth_role`).
- `SuperAdminAuth` on `purge` ⇒ `require_super_admin()`: `Role::Admin` **and**
  an unrestricted `ActScope`. Decided through `ActScope`, never
  `allowed_contexts.is_empty()`.
- No context scoping existed on any of the four, so none was lost.

**Two differences, both in the stricter direction.** (1) The ACL row is read now
rather than when the session was minted, so a row removed, demoted or expired
since login refuses here and would not have refused on the bearer route — there
is a test for it. (2) Revocation granularity changes: a bearer session is killed
by revoking the session, a signed document by removing or expiring the ACL row,
which is the only authority it ever rested on.

The generated payload is also schema-validated (`validate_value`), which the
bearer routes' hand-written bodies are not, and each success reply is asserted
against its published `#response` schema — the router's `response_conformance`
layer keys on the `Trust-Task` header, which the document endpoint does not use,
so it does not reach these replies.

**Two properties of the door itself, worth knowing before adopting it.**
`POST /v1/trust-tasks` sits on the governed unauth chain, so these calls are
rate-limited per source IP (5/s, burst 10) and capped at 64 KiB rather than the
main chain's 1 MB. Neither changes anything today — every client still uses the
bearer routes — but a `members/update` carrying a large `extensions` bag will
fit on one door and not the other.

## The accepted-id record

The claim is the spine's: `dispatch_trust_task_core` claims before
`dispatch_typed` and settles after (`completed` on success, `release` on
failure), so every one of these arms is inside it — claim → execute → settle,
not check-then-act.

**The bearer routes are not routed through it, and that is not the hole §6a
warns about.** They take a flat payload and a JWT, not a document: they have no
`id` to claim, and a captured signed document cannot be presented at them at all
because no body shape there would carry it. The two doors are disjoint in
credential type, so there is nothing for them to share. A future batch that put
a task on a *second document* binding would have to claim through
`state.accepted_ids()` like the spine does.

## The bearer routes stay, with a stated removal point

All four remain mounted, each now carrying the transitional note in its OpenAPI
description. **The admin SPA cannot sign.** `vtc-service/admin-ui/src` contains
no signing primitive at all — no `eddsa-jcs-2022`, no Ed25519, no
`crypto.subtle.sign` — and its second factor is a passkey, which is WebAuthn and
cannot produce a Data-Integrity proof. So the console holds no key with which to
author a Trust Task document, and retiring its routes now would take the member
surface out of the admin UI. The removal point is: when the console can author a
DI-signed Trust Task document, its four routes go in the same change.

Clients checked, none broken because nothing was removed:

- **admin SPA** — uses all four (`plugins/members.tsx`). Unchanged.
- **`vtc-client`** — `member_credentials`, `update_member_extensions`,
  `remove_member` hit three of the four over bearer REST. Unchanged.
- **`cnm-cli`** — reaches none of the four (only `members/list`, via
  `vtc-client::list_members`). Unchanged.

`admin-ui/openapi.json` and `src/lib/wire.ts` are regenerated for the
description changes.

## Tests

`vtc-service/src/trust_tasks/mod.rs::members_admin_tests`, named for the
requirements:

- `vti_ops_020_a_signed_admin_document_reads_member_credentials` — accepted,
  answered in the task's own response shape.
- `vti_ops_020_an_unsigned_admin_document_is_refused` — all four, `proofRequired`,
  and no effect happened.
- `a_non_admin_signer_is_refused_every_admin_member_verb`,
  `a_signer_with_no_acl_row_is_refused`,
  `an_expired_admin_acl_row_no_longer_authorizes` — the `AdminAuth` gate.
- `a_context_scoped_admin_may_not_purge` / `…may_still_read_credentials` — the
  `SuperAdminAuth` gate, and that it was not copied one notch too tight.
- `an_unknown_member_is_the_declared_not_found`,
  `update_still_refuses_promotion_to_admin`,
  `an_omitted_extensions_member_does_not_clear_the_bag` — the operations' own
  refusals, on this door too.
- `vti_ops_025_a_redelivered_document_is_answered_not_re_executed`,
  `vti_ops_026_a_different_document_under_a_spent_id_conflicts`,
  `vti_ops_027_the_spent_id_is_visible_to_any_binding` — driven through `purge`,
  because a second execution is only visible at a verb with an effect.
- `every_moved_task_declares_the_proof_these_tests_assume` — the premise, so a
  registry relaxation fails here first.

`the_dispatched_set_declares_the_proofs_the_design_note_records` moves 20 → 24,
and the design note records the batch (§2, §6b) so a future batch that lands
without updating it fails a test.

## Next batch

`vtc/join-requests/decide/0.1` and `vtc/community/profile/update/0.1` — the same
admin-from-ACL shape, the same console dependency.
`vtc/admin/invites/{create,revoke}` would round it out, but `vtc/invitations/*`
is owned by another change at the time of writing.

title: fix(vta-service): a consent refusal sheds its relay copies, not its coordinates
body:
## Keyring VTI-37

Reported by the Keyring team (Berkman Center, Keyring wallet).

**Symptom.** A task held for consent is refused `auth:consent_required`. With three or more approvers, the refusal's `details` was missing entirely: the requester got a bare code, with no `payloadDigest`, no `correlator`, no `challenge`, and nothing to relay.

**Root cause.** The annex (built in `policy_gate.rs`) carries the ceremony's coordinates plus `consentRequests`: one VTA-signed `task-consent/request` per approver, each with the effects diff, for the requester to relay when the VTA has no route to an approver. Each request is about 1 KB. `bound_details` (`helpers.rs`) holds every rejection `details` to the framework's **default** bound (Trust Tasks SPEC §8.2.2: 4096 bytes of JCS and 16 members; no spec declares this shape, so the default applies), and it was all-or-nothing. At three approvers the annex went over, and the whole of it was dropped.

## What changed

- `bound_details` now **degrades before it drops**. A table, `SHEDDABLE_DETAILS_MEMBERS`, lists members that can be shed, in order, each paired with a count member that replaces it: `consentRequests` → `consentRequestsOmitted`. Members are shed until the annex fits. If it still doesn't fit, the whole annex is dropped as before. Leaving members out to stay within the bound conforms; going over it does not.
- `consentRequests` goes out **whole or not at all**. A partial list would read as the approver set, and a requester relaying to only the ones it got would silently skip the rest. The count says the relay copies exist but didn't fit, which is different from saying there were none.
- The core members (reason, payloadDigest, correlator, challenge, approverSet, minApprovals, excludeRequester) always go out. They are a few hundred bytes.
- Other rejections are unchanged: none of them carries a sheddable member. The `reject_with_code` funnel gets the same behaviour.
- The warn log now names what was shed, or says the whole annex was dropped even after shedding.
- `docs/02-vta/task-consent.md` documents the bound and the omission count.

**Additivity (`consentRequestsOmitted`).** No Rust consumer deserializes this `details` into a typed struct. `vta-sdk`'s `trust_task_error` reads it member by member through `Value::get`, so it has no `deny_unknown_fields` problem. The browser plugin (`packages/core/src/vta/request-task.ts`) already treats a missing `consentRequests` as `[]`. trust-tasks-rs does not type it either. No OpenAPI or wire.ts snapshot covers this annex.

**Consequence.** When the count is present, the requester cannot relay. The approvers hear about the request only from the VTA's own push. The spec follow-up below closes that gap.

## Planned spec follow-up (not in this PR)

- Declare the `auth:consent_required` details fragment in `task-consent/_shared`, with its own bound and the omission member. Today it relies on the framework default.
- Add `task-consent/pending/0.1`, which fetches a pending request's signed requests by `correlator`, so a requester that got `consentRequestsOmitted` can still relay.

## Tests

- `cargo test -p vta-service --lib`: 1269 pass, 1 ignored (full run, including the produced-URI census). `trust_tasks::helpers` alone: 24 pass. Three are new:
  - consent-shaped annex with 1, 2, 3 and 5 approvers: core members are always present; requests are present whole when they fit, otherwise omitted with the count; JCS is always ≤ 4096 bytes and there are always ≤ 16 members
  - shedding on the extended-code funnel
  - an annex still too large after shedding is dropped whole
- `cargo test -p vta-service --features webvh --test delegated_consent_e2e`: 9 pass. The new one, `a_consent_refusal_keeps_its_coordinates_however_many_approvers`, sends real VTA-signed requests over the router for 1, 2, 3 and 5 approvers and asserts the same invariants. It also checks that shedding starts at 2 or 3 approvers and not at 1.
- `cargo clippy -p vta-service --all-targets -D warnings` (default and `webvh`), `cargo fmt`.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1): n/a
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, all consumers (incl. JS) checked (R3.*): `consentRequestsOmitted` is additive, see above
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*): n/a
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*): the warn log says what was shed
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutation
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged: none

The REST `ApprovalRequired` body is not bounded by this (it isn't a Trust Task error payload) and is unchanged.

title: docs(vtc): changing a community's transports after mint; console sign-in says which identity it presents
body:
Two findings from Keyring, the external team at the Berkman Center that builds the Keyring wallet.

## VTI-12: changing a community's transports after mint

**Root cause.** Since #1632 (`cnm did-log install`, `did-management/did/register/0.1`), a serverless VTC can take a log the VTA extended. The docs still called its `did.jsonl` "write-once" and said transports and referrals were "fixed at mint". So did the `vtc setup` prompts, the example setup TOML and the `vtc-host` template description. The working flow was only written down in pieces: `cnm-cli/src/did_log.rs` module docs, the `pnm` redeploy hint, and one line in each of two docs.

**Changed**
- `docs/03-vtc/community-lifecycle.md` has a new section, **Changing the community's transports after mint**, a walkthrough with every command and flag checked against the clap definitions:
  - `pnm did-mgmt dids get` (`Server: serverless` or a server id)
  - `pnm did-mgmt dids edit --did`, and the `#tsp` entry's shape (`serviceEndpoint` is the mediator DID)
  - `pnm did-mgmt dids get-log <did> --out did.jsonl`
  - `cnm [--url <base>] [-c <slug>] did-log install --file did.jsonl`
- The section explains the serverless vs DID-host difference. A VTC on a DID host needs only the edit: the VTA pushes the new entry to the host, and `cnm did-log install` refuses a DID with a path. After install, `vtc status` compares the document with the build, and the section lists the caveats: `[messaging]`, the mediator must route the protocol, and keep `#didcomm` when adding `#tsp`.
- Stale write-once claims are replaced with pointers to that section in:
  - `docs/02-vta/did-templates.md`, `docs/05-design-notes/vtc-mvp.md`, `docs/03-vtc/examples/vtc-setup.example.toml`
  - `vtc setup` prompts, the `from_toml` docs and error text
  - the `vta-sdk` `transports.rs` module docs and the `vtc-host.json` description
- `runtime-service-management.md` links the walkthrough.
- `pnm did-mgmt dids get-log --help` no longer says the log is a "snapshot from provisioning time" or that it runs without a session. It returns the VTA's current log through the authenticated client.

## Q13: console wallet sign-in buttons present different identities

**Root cause.** The ACL admits a DID, and the two wallet buttons can present different DIDs, but the labels didn't say so.
- "Sign in with VTA wallet" calls `vtaWallet.login()`. The wallet presents the persona bound to this site if there is one. Otherwise it asks, and one answer it offers is its own holder `did:key`. Wallets older than vta-browser-plugin#146 always present the holder key.
- "Sign in via VTA-proxied SIOP" calls `walletProfile` + `proxyLogin`. It always presents a VTA-held `did-self-issued` persona, which the VTA signs for.

An admin whose ACL entry names their VTA identity can count on only the second button.

**Changed** (`vtc-service/admin-ui`)
- New labels, each with a line underneath:
  - **Sign in with this browser's wallet**: "The wallet presents the identity it uses for this site — its own key (a did:key) unless you have chosen a VTA identity here."
  - **Sign in as a VTA identity**: "Your VTA signs as the identity bound to this community. Use this when your ACL entry names your VTA identity."
  - The lead text and "Sign in as a different VTA identity…" are updated to match.
- A refused VTA-identity sign-in now shows the DID it presented, with the `vtc admin invite --did <did>` fix. It does this on every attempt, not only the first (`SignInAsError`), and on the hand-picked-entry path too.
- A refused browser-wallet sign-in can't name the DID, because the wallet doesn't report it on failure. Instead its hint points at the VTA-identity button.

## Tests
- admin-ui: `npm run lint` (wire:check + `tsc -b`), `npx vitest run` (172 pass, including a new `wallet.test.ts` checking the refusal carries the presented DID), and `vite build`. CI builds the bundle through `vtc-service/build.rs` into `OUT_DIR`, so no committed assets change.
- `cargo clippy -p vta-sdk -p pnm-cli -p vtc-service --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `cargo test -p vta-sdk --lib did_templates`, `cargo test -p vtc-service --lib setup`, `cargo test -p cnm-cli`, `cargo test -p pnm-cli`

`docs/03-vtc/credential-delivery.md` and `vtc-service/src/messaging.rs` are untouched; another PR owns them.

title: feat(vtc,room-host): warn on unknown and misplaced config keys (Keyring VTI-06)
body:
## Finding

Keyring VTI-06 (Berkman Center Keyring wallet team) reported that a config key appended below the last `[table]` header of a generated `mediator.toml` had no effect and produced no message. The mediator fix is in affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#886. This PR closes the same gap in VTI services that still parsed their config with plain `toml::from_str`.

## Root cause

`vtc-service` `AppConfig::load` used `toml::from_str`, which drops keys the schema does not recognise. Only `[secrets]` had `deny_unknown_fields`. A typo, a removed setting, or a key filed under the wrong table because of TOML table scoping all took no effect, and nothing said so. The VTA already handles this (`vta-config`: `serde_ignored` in `load`, warnings in `validate`).

## What changed

- **vtc-service**: a new `AppConfig::load_with_unknown_keys` returns `(AppConfig, Vec<String>)` and parses through `serde_ignored`. `load` keeps its signature and delegates to it. `AppConfig::warn_unknown_keys(&[String])` logs one warning per key. The daemon calls it right after `init_tracing`, because loading runs before the subscriber exists. Each message names the full path, e.g. `join_requests.allowed_origins`, and notes that a key placed after a `[table]` header belongs to that table. Keys are reported, never rejected.
- **room-host**: the `--secrets` file is parsed the same way and warns inline, since tracing is already up at that point. This one matters: a typo'd `[secret]` table used to leave the plaintext default backend in place without a word. `serde_ignored` is optional and turned on by the `didcomm`/`onboarding` features alongside `toml`.
- Not in this workspace and not changed: did-hosting (affinidi-webvh-service) and vti-push-gateway.
- `AppConfig`'s fields are unchanged; the change is two new methods. Storing the keys on the struct was avoided on purpose: a public field breaks external struct literals (`tests/routing_cors.rs` has one), and a private field makes the struct impossible to build outside the crate, which is also breaking. No `version =` edits (release-plz owns them).

## Tests

- `cargo test -p vtc-service --lib config::` (24): a key appended after the last table is reported with its dotted path and the table-scoping hint; a top-level typo is reported plainly; a valid config (including the `community_name` alias) reports nothing; a config written by `save()` reloads with no unknown keys.
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --test routing_cors` (19).
- `cargo test -p room-host --features didcomm,onboarding --bin room-host` (2): a misplaced table is reported; a valid file reports nothing.
- `cargo clippy -D warnings --all-targets`: vtc-service, and room-host both with and without `didcomm,onboarding`. `cargo fmt --all`.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a, no clients
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1): n/a, read-only parsing
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*): none; `unknown_keys` is `serde(skip)`
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*): unchanged; unknown keys are advisory and never loosen anything
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*): the warning reports exactly the path serde ignored
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" (R2.1): n/a, no mutations
- [x] Deviations: none

title: feat(vetting/attestation): the four tasks hidden-vetter admission needs
body:
Four specifications for **hidden-vetter admission**: a community can require that *k* distinct
vetters vetted an applicant, count that requirement with the rule it already uses, and never
learn which of its members did the vetting.

The applicant proves it. The vetter attests under a blind class credential and spends a token to
do so, which is what keeps an anonymous attestation rate-limited. What was missing was the wire,
and these are it.

### The four

| Task | Who → whom | What it settles |
|---|---|---|
| `vtc/vetting/vetters/pcs-root/0.1` | vetter → community | Enrolment for a class label. The community checks its own records — a live vetter grant, no credential under this label yet, the identifier this member was bound to — then signs a commitment it cannot open. |
| `vtc/vetting/vetters/pcs-tokens/0.1` | vetter → community | One tick of the attestation-token drip, at the community's published rate. |
| `vetting/attestation/0.1` | vetter → applicant | The facts of the session, with no issuer. |
| `vtc/vetting/pcs-challenge/0.1` | applicant → community | The single-use nonce the proof must bind. |

### Three decisions worth review

**The drip is unconditional.** A vetter asks on a schedule whether or not it has vetted anyone,
because a fetch that happened only when someone was busy would announce that they were busy. The
quota is the community's to enforce, stated as a conformance requirement rather than left to the
asker's restraint: a batch over the published rate is refused before anything is signed.

**`vetting/attestation` declares `identifierScope: any`,** and says a consumer **MUST NOT** record
the delivering `issuer` beside the attestation. The delivering identity is deliberately not what
makes an attestation count — recording it would rebuild, in the applicant's own store, exactly the
link the exchange removes. Nothing here needs a reusable identifier: the community never sees the
document, and the applicant only needs the identifier the session was held under, so a pair that
runs the whole vetting exchange pairwise loses nothing.

**Dates, not timestamps,** on the attested statement's validity window. An exact time would let a
community line an attestation up with a vetter's activity, which undoes the proof without touching
it.

### Mechanics

- Bindings regenerated for all four languages; `npm run check-bindings` agrees (481 specs).
- Each task declares its error codes; each response is titled so the TypeScript binding exports
  a `Response` type.
- `payload.invalid-examples.json` is not included yet — happy to add fixtures for the negative
  space if reviewers want them before merge.

Implemented against these schemas in both halves of a VTC deployment; the implementation carries
the payload types by hand and validates them against these files until a `trust-tasks-rs` release
serves them.

title: chore(deps): take affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.26.27 (cross-mediator TSP accept, send retry)
body:
Picks up two TSP fixes from Keyring's round-3 findings. This PR changes only the lockfile: the manifests' `0.26.12` floor already admits 0.26.27, so no `version =` field changes.

- **0.26.26** (affinidi-tdk-rs #883), for **VTI-39**: when a connection drops mid-send (`IncompleteMessage`, reset), `send_raw` re-POSTs the *same* sealed bytes up to twice. It never re-seals, so the mediator's store dedup (sha256 of the stored bytes) keeps exactly one copy. It never retries an HTTP status. Each request now has a 30 s timeout. Before this, a VTA that completed a task over TSP could lose its reply to one stale pooled socket.
- **0.26.27** (affinidi-tdk-rs #884), for **VTI-41**: a routed reply or control frame whose route starts at another mediator is now sent through the sender's own mediator first. Our own mediator used to refuse it as a non-local recipient, so no TSP relationship could form across two mediators. The receiving mediator must still admit relayed hops, either with `enable_inter_mediator_relay` or with the sending mediator on `relay_trusted_mediators`.

Companion to #1675 (VTI-43, per-sender ordering), which is already merged.

**Lockfile note:** `cargo update -p affinidi-messaging-sdk` also re-selected `syn`/`base64` for three unrelated crates. Main's lockfile passes `cargo metadata --locked` without those changes, so I left them out. The diff is just the SDK entry and its new `hyper` dependency.

**Tested:** these e2e TSP suites all pass with `--locked`: `tsp_vta_trust_task` (12), `tsp_vtaclient_relate` (11), `tsp_dual_client_reply` (10), `tsp_self_repair_on_drop` (10), `tsp_round_trip` (13).

* feat(vetting/attestation): the four tasks hidden-vetter admission needs

A community can hide which of its vetters vetted an applicant: the vetter
attests under a blind class credential, the applicant proves that k distinct
holders of one attested it, and the community counts the proof with the rule
it already counts named statements with. What was missing was the wire.

Four specifications, and the split between them is the design:

  community checks its own records (a live vetter grant, no credential under

  and no issuer. The delivering identity is deliberately NOT what makes it
  count, and a consumer is told not to record it beside the attestation: that
  would recreate, in the applicant's own store, the link the exchange removes.
- vtc/vetting/pcs-challenge — the applicant asks the community for the
  single-use nonce its proof must bind. Without it a proof verifies as often
  as it is submitted, and the second submission counts as readily as the first.

vetting/attestation declares identifierScope: any. Nothing in it needs a
reusable identifier — the community never sees the document, and the applicant

title: Close the dispatcher-leniency entry in the divergence register
body:
The second of the three entries #35 recorded in Appendix F.2 is resolved. It
leaves the table and is recorded in **F.5 Closed**, in the form #37 uses: the
row is `| Requirement | Closed by |`, the second column states the behaviour
rather than naming an implementation or a change, and the `*(observed)*`
qualifier does not travel with it, because F.5's row form does not carry one.
One row out, one row in.

#37 left this entry open on purpose, and said exactly what would close it. At
that point the acceptance window and the required time of issue were already
unconditional, and the proof requirement was unconditional on the HTTP binding
but gated on the messaging transports by `[trust_tasks]
require_declared_proof`, default `false` — because one client built five of
those documents with no proof attached. "It should close when the flag's
default flips, and that is one line then." That has happened:
OpenVTC/openvtc-core#371 signs all five, and
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1672 (merged 23 September 2026)
deletes the flag. **Those numbers are in the commit message rather than in the
row**, for the reason F.6 gives and #37 followed.

## What was checked, in the merged tree

Not taken from the change's own description.

- **The dispatcher enforces the registry's policy unmodified.**
  `spec_policy_for(&type_uri).enforce(&doc)` runs against the published policy
  — `proof` REQUIRED, `recipient` REQUIRED, `issuedAt` REQUIRED, audience
  binding — with no narrowing in between.
  `narrow_for_transitional_allowance`, which implemented the old relaxation by
  narrowing the *value* rather than skipping the call, does not exist anywhere
  in the crate. The dispatcher reads config for one thing now, the node's own
  DID.
- **A config carrying the retired key is answered, not ignored.**
  `= false` fails to deserialize, and the refusal sits in the deserializer so
  it holds on every path that parses the config rather than only the daemon's
  boot path. `= true` parses, warns at load and starts — it asked for what is
  now the only behaviour, so the operator's intent is intact and only the line
  is stale. The field is `skip_serializing`, so a config the service writes
  back never hands it over again. There is no value that keeps the old
  behaviour.
- **The window and the required time of issue are in the same spine as the
  proof check**, ahead of any transport-specific work: a 10-minute maximum age
  with 60s skew, `issuedAt` required, one clock reading for every temporal
  decision so the acceptance window and the replay record's retention cannot
  land on opposite sides of the same bound. REST (`POST /v1/trust-tasks`),
  task-typed DIDComm, enveloped DIDComm and TSP all reach it through
  `dispatch_trust_task_core`.
- **The tests that asserted the old allowance were rewritten, not deleted.**
  Three single-transport tests — the REST refusal, the DIDComm allowance under
  the default, and the DIDComm refusal with the flag on — became one that
  drives a single unsigned document over REST, DIDComm **and** TSP and demands
  a refusal on each, plus a signed control, without which the first would pass
  equally on a node that refused every DIDComm and TSP document outright. Four
  config tests cover the retired key. Each rewrite says in the code why its
  conclusion moved.

## Two things the row records beyond the entry's resolution

- **A proof is now bound to the document's own `issuer`.** A proof that
  verifies under a key that issuer does not control is refused rather than
  satisfying the requirement — previously any verifying proof did, which
  established that somebody signed something and not who composed the request.
  That is tighter than the entry asked for, so the row says so.
- **The bearer-route entry is not closed by this**, and I have left it exactly
  where it is. The ~48 tasks it records are served over an HTTP binding that
  carries no operation document at all; they never reach the dispatcher, so
  none of this reaches them. Its own resolution said the dispatcher had to
  enforce *before* moving anything into it — "moving a task into a dispatcher
  that does not enforce its proof requirement moves the divergence instead of
  closing it". The row ends by saying this is that precondition and not that
  entry's resolution, so closing one cannot be read as closing the other.

## One thing I did not change

F.5's preamble says "Two of the entries below were closed by changes whose own
limits are worth carrying", and names the two by their mechanism. This row
carries a limit too, of a different kind — a statement of scope about a
*different* entry rather than a limit inherent to the change — so I left the
sentence alone rather than editing prose the working group wrote to make a
count come out. Say the word and I will fold it in here or in #37.

## Mechanics

Branched from `main`, not stacked on #37. The two entries are independent
facts closed by independent changes, and the working group may take them in
either order or not at all; stacking would put #37's row in this diff and tie
this one's fate to it. The cost is a likely conflict in the F.5 table and in
the adjacent F.2 deletions, which is two rows kept and one line each removed —
whoever merges second resolves it.

`npm run render` completes and `docs/index.html` carries the moved row under
F.5, with no trace of it in F.2 and the bearer-route entry untouched. No other
file changes.

  deserialize, on every path that parses the config; `= true` warns at load
  and starts, because it asked for what is now the only behaviour. So an
  operator cannot silently keep the old behaviour.
- The acceptance window and the required time of issue are applied in the
  same spine, before any transport-specific work, and REST, DIDComm and TSP
  all reach it through the same entry point.
- The tests that pinned the old allowance were rewritten, not deleted: one
  unsigned document is now refused on all three transports, with a signed
  control so the refusal cannot be a transport outage passing as compliance.

The row records two things beyond the entry's own resolution. A proof is now
bound to the document's own issuer, which is tighter than the entry asked for.
And the bearer-route entry (VTI-OPS-020/021/024/093) is not closed by this and
stays where it is: those tasks never reach the dispatcher.

`npm run render` completes and `docs/index.html` carries the moved row under
F.5 with no trace of it in F.2. No other file changes.

title: feat(vtc): the accepted-id record is shared across bindings (VTI-OPS-027)
body:
Refs #1641. Phase 2 groundwork. **No route moves here.**

## Why this is its own PR

[#1659](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1659) made the Trust Task dispatcher enforce what a specification declares — proof required, recipient required, an `issuedAt` acceptance window, and a replay record so a document id cannot be accepted twice. Its design note (`docs/05-design-notes/vtc-trust-task-proof-enforcement.md`) then flags one thing that has to be true before phase 2 can start:

> **VTI-OPS-027** requires the accepted-identifier record to be shared across every binding. Today's `REPLAY_GUARD` is process-local and covers only the document dispatcher, so a task served on both the bearer route and the dispatcher would have a record on one binding and none on the other.

Phase 2 moves ~49 tasks that are served only as flat-payload REST behind a bearer JWT onto the dispatcher, and keeps the bearer routes as a documented transitional path while the admin SPA, `cnm` and `vtc-client` migrate. So for the length of that migration each of those tasks has **two** doors. With a per-binding record, replay protection is defeated by presenting the captured document at the other one — which is exactly the case VTI-OPS-027's rationale names:

> A document captured from one binding — a log, a proxy, a stored message — is a well-formed, correctly signed, correctly addressed document, and the second binding has no reason to doubt it. Where the two bindings do not share a record, the node's replay protection is exactly as good as its least-used transport.

Doing this in the same PR as the first batch would mean the migration opens the hole. Hence: precondition, not migration.

## What changed

**The record is now `vtc-service/src/trust_tasks/accepted_ids.rs`, backed by a new `accepted_ids` keyspace.** Any binding reaches it as `AppState::accepted_ids()` — cheap to construct, nothing to thread through:

```rust
match state.accepted_ids().claim(&doc, retain_until, now).await {
    Ok(Acceptance::Fresh(claim)) => { /* execute, then claim.completed(..) / claim.release() */ }
    Ok(Acceptance::Duplicate { prior_response, in_flight }) => /* answer with the recorded outcome */,
    Ok(Acceptance::Conflict) => /* idConflict */,
    Err(e) => /* e.reject_reason() — internalError or unavailable */,
}
```

`AcceptedClaim` is `#[must_use]` and warns on drop if it was neither completed nor released — an early `?` between the claim and the effect would otherwise burn the document id silently for the rest of the window, which is the shape a REST handler makes.

**What a replayed id answers is unchanged**, and is what SPEC §7.2 (*Disposition of a duplicate*) asks for:

| arrival | answer |
|---|---|
| same document, first execution finished | the recorded response, `200` |
| same document, original still running | `202` — "return or expose the existing execution state rather than begin another" |
| same document, specification defines no success response | `204` |
| **different** document under the spent id | `idConflict` |
| record unreadable | `unavailable` (retryable) — fail closed |

Never `taskFailed`: "the task did not fail, it already happened."

**Bounded and swept.** #1659's `retain_until` cap is unchanged — a producer-chosen `expiresAt` still cannot pin an id past `issuedAt + max_age + skew`. Two things the move required: `accepted_ids::sweep_expired` now runs on the retention sweeper's tick (the in-memory guard was bounded by capacity eviction; a keyspace is not), and a claim whose caller bounds nothing is bounded here rather than written as a row with no deadline. A test pins that fallback to `freshness_policy()`'s actual window so the two cannot drift.

Two properties come free: the record survives a restart, and it is no longer capacity-evicted — a burst of distinct documents could previously push a live record out before its deadline and let a replay through.

## The atomicity question, answered honestly

**Claim-and-insert is atomic within the process. It is not cross-replica.**

A claim is not one store operation. An expired record must be treated as absent — otherwise a released id conflicts forever with a document nobody would execute — so the path is read → remove-if-expired → insert. `KeyspaceHandle::insert_if_absent` is atomic and is what writes the record, but it cannot settle that sequence: two callers racing on an expired record can each remove and each insert, the second removing the first's live record, and both come away `Fresh`. That is the TOCTOU #1656 closed on the authenticate path, in another costume.

It is closed here by a striped async mutex held across the claim. Its scope is the process, which is the whole scope in which two claims can race today: fjall holds an exclusive lock on the store directory, so a second process cannot open the same store. That is the same scope as the store's own per-keyspace write locks, which is what `insert_if_absent`, `take_raw` and `swap` serialise on.

**What it would take to be cross-replica:** a shared *store*, not a shared lock. No networked store backend exists for the VTC (`vti_common::store::Store` is fjall or the enclave's vsock proxy, and the VTC never targets TEE). When one does, the right fix is a native conditional write at the store layer — Redis `SET NX` / `GETDEL`, DynamoDB `ConditionExpression` / `DeleteItem ReturnValues=ALL_OLD` — behind a new `KeyspaceHandle` primitive, at which point `claim` becomes a single call to it and the mutex goes. A replicated VTC would double-execute until then, which is a deployment this service does not support for several other reasons (the in-memory session map, the member-count cache, the rate limiter). Said so in the module doc and in §6a of the design note rather than left to be found.

## What phase 2's first batch must then do

At each migrating site: take the claim **before** the effect, settle it after, and refuse `Conflict` as `idConflict`. Not "check whether the id was seen" — a check-then-act at the route is the TOCTOU the claim exists to close. The bearer route and the dispatcher arm both go through `AppState::accepted_ids()`, so a document accepted on one is refused on the other, which is VTI-OPS-027 met rather than restated.

## Tests

New, in `accepted_ids` (11): a replayed id is a duplicate carrying the recorded outcome (`vti_ops_025_*`); an in-flight duplicate; a different document under a spent id is a conflict; a released claim frees the id; an expired record is treated as absent and the sweep purges it (`vti_ops_026_*`); concurrent presentation of one id yields exactly one claim, including over an expired record; **a second binding over the same keyspace sees what the first accepted** (`vti_ops_027_*`); an unbounded claim is bounded; and the fallback retention is pinned to the acceptance window.

`spine_proof_tests` is **unmodified** — every #1659 assertion passes against the store-backed record, including the replay and conflict pair, which now exercise the new path end to end.

One deliberate behaviour change: the dispatcher's arm for "a `ReplayVerdict` variant this build does not know" is gone. `Acceptance` is this crate's own enum rather than the library's `#[non_exhaustive]` one, so a new variant is a compile error at that match — the stronger form of the same guard.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast` (admin UI built, not skipped) — exit 0
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean

Rebased onto `origin/main` (7dc69d8) and the VTC job re-run after the rebase.

title: security(persona)!: the correlation answer on a local write is the holder's
body:
Stacked on #1673 (`fix/persona-holder-is-granted-not-inherited`), because it uses the same `is_holder` predicate. Retarget to main when that merges.

Two defects in one task. The second was found by writing a test for the first.

### 1. A probe oracle across the context boundary

`persona/local/profile/put` is **context-scoped**, and its response carried:

```json
"correlation": { "severity": "high", "matchesPoolValue": true }
```

`matchesPoolValue` is computed from the holder's **agent-wide** blinded index — does any attribute in the pool hold this exact value. A caller that can write is a caller that can guess, so any application authorized in one context had an unbounded oracle over the whole pool: one guess per write, each answer confirming or eliminating one.

No value crosses the boundary and none needs to. For a name, an address or a date of birth, **confirming a guess is disclosure**, and the guesser is inside a single context learning about all of them. The schema's own description said the index "is above the boundary, is keyed by a hash, and only the holder can query it" — while this response answered it to anyone in the context.

The member is now included only for a caller that passes the holder test, and **omitted rather than softened**: a coarser signal is still an oracle, only a slower one. The holder loses nothing — the audit row records the flag whoever asked, and `persona/correlation/analyze` answers it properly. Made conditional in the specification first, in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#609.

### 2. A payload the SDK could not make conform

Writing that test produced the agent refusing its own SDK's request:

> Additional properties are not allowed ('provenance' was unexpected)

`LocalProfileEntry` reused the pool's `InlineValue`, whose `provenance` is **required** — and the schema has no `provenance` for a context-local entry, with `additionalProperties: false`. So **every** local-profile write `persona_local_profile_put` could build was rejected. The feature openvtc and the console were built on has never worked.

`LocalInlineValue` is that type without the member. Its absence is the boundary, not an omission: a `credentialBacked` provenance names a `credentialId` and a `claimPath`, and a value authored inside a context has nowhere to put either, so carrying the member would let a context assert a value is attested when no credential was ever checked.

This is what the workspace rule against hand-writing a payload type for a task with a generated module exists to prevent — the generated type never had the member. The plugin's copy of the same bug is OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin#271; openvtc's follows once this publishes.

### Tests

- `the_correlation_flag_on_a_local_write_is_answered_only_to_the_holder` — holder is told, context-scoped caller gets no `correlation` member at all, using the second identity added in #1673.
- `a_context_local_entry_carries_no_provenance` — pins the wire shape in the SDK.

CI set run locally: fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, workspace (4821), vtc (1865).

title: fix(vta-service): answer a TSP relationship request before its sender's later traffic
body:
Keyring **VTI-43**.

## Diagnosis

A phone sent a TSP relationship invite (XRFI), then 16 ms later a Trust Task. `run_inbound_loop` reads frames in order but `tokio::spawn`s each (semaphore, 32), with no per-sender ordering. The task's reply (~2 ms, a `permissionDenied`) went out ~328 ms **before** the VTA finished answering the invite. `accept_relationship` resolves the peer VID and POSTs XRFA, and only then marks the relationship Bidirectional. The phone admits application messages only on a bidirectional relationship, so it dropped the reply. When the accept won the race, everything worked.

## Fix

This adds `vta-service/src/messaging/sender_order.rs`. It orders inbound frames per authenticated sender. The order is taken **on the reader task, before spawning**: two spawned tasks would reach a lock in whatever order the scheduler runs them, not in arrival order.

- A TSP relationship-control frame is a **barrier**. It runs after every earlier barrier from the same sender.
- TSP application frames **follow**. They run after every earlier barrier from their sender, but they don't wait for each other. A barrier also doesn't wait for earlier application frames. This is deliberate: with a plain per-sender FIFO, a Trust Task waiting on a later message from the same peer (for example a step-up approval) would deadlock.
- Frames from different senders never wait on each other. DIDComm stays unordered, as before.
- **Bounded.** The map holds only senders that have a barrier in flight, and an entry is removed when its last barrier finishes. Each wait times out after 15 s (R1.3), so a hung accept falls back to the old unordered behaviour for the frames behind it instead of stranding the peer.
- A barrier releases the frames behind it on drop, so a failure or panic releases them too.

**vtc-service needs no change.** Its inbound loop awaits `handle_tsp` inline, so it already handles each frame in arrival order.

## Tests

- `sender_order` unit tests use deterministic gating (a oneshot stands in for the slow accept):
  - the reply waits for the earlier accept;
  - a control case with no barrier shows the reply overtaking (the bug);
  - other senders aren't blocked;
  - followers run concurrently;
  - barriers chain in arrival order, whatever the spawn order;
  - a panicking barrier releases the frames behind it;
  - a hung barrier is bounded;
  - anonymous frames are unordered;
  - finished barriers are evicted.
- `frame_order` classification tests: TSP control is a barrier, TSP traffic follows, DIDComm is unordered.
- I didn't add a hermetic e2e test. `MockVta` has no way to add latency to the accept path, and the Rust client's session waits for the accept inside `relate()`, so the race can't be reproduced there reliably. The existing TSP e2e binaries still pass: `tsp_vta_trust_task`, `tsp_dual_client_reply`, `tsp_vtaclient_relate`, `tsp_self_repair_on_drop`.

`cargo clippy -p vta-service --all-targets -D warnings` is clean under the default feature set and under the three reduced sets CI uses. `cargo fmt` is clean.

## Checklist (vti-stack-development-guide)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): the std mutex is only held for map bookkeeping, and the barrier wait is time-bounded
- [x] No new HTTP clients; no wire types changed; no retries added
- [x] No version edits

title: feat(vtc): the accepted-id record is shared across bindings (VTI-OPS-027) (#1674)
body:
feat(vtc): the accepted-id record is shared across bindings (VTI-OPS-027) (#1674)

VTI-OPS-027 requires the record of accepted document identifiers to be
shared across every binding a node exposes: "A document accepted on one
binding MUST NOT be acceptable on another." #1659 left that record as a
process-local `InMemoryReplayGuard` reachable only from the Trust Task
dispatcher, which is adequate while the dispatcher is the only door.

only as flat-payload REST behind a bearer JWT onto the dispatcher, and
the bearer routes stay as a transitional path while the admin SPA, `cnm`
and `vtc-client` migrate. A task reachable through both doors would keep
a record on one and none on the other, and the specification's own
rationale says what that is worth: "the node's replay protection is
exactly as good as its least-used transport." So this has to land
before the first batch, not with it — otherwise the migration opens the
hole it exists to close.

The record is now `crate::trust_tasks::accepted_ids`, backed by the new

settled with `AcceptedClaim::{completed, release}`, and the claim is
`#[must_use]` and warns on drop if it is neither — an early `?` between
the claim and the effect would otherwise burn the document id silently.
Each phase-2 call site is that match, not a redesign.

What a replayed id answers is unchanged, and is what SPEC §7.2
(*Disposition of a duplicate*) asks for: the same document again is
answered with the recorded response (or `202` while the original is
still running, `204` where the specification defines none), never
`taskFailed` — "the task did not fail, it already happened". A
*different* document under a spent id is `idConflict`.

Two properties fall out of moving into the store: the record survives a
restart, and it is no longer capacity-evicted — the in-memory guard
could push a live record out under a burst of distinct documents and let
a replay through. What does not fall out is a bound, so

expired record can each remove and each insert, which is the TOCTOU

title: Close the admin-promotion entry in the divergence register
body:
One of the three entries #35 recorded in Appendix F.2 has been resolved. It
leaves the table and is recorded in **F.5 Closed**, which is what the register
says it does with a divergence that has been closed ("An entry leaves the tables
above when the divergence is closed, and is recorded here so that a reader can
tell a register that is being worked from one that has been abandoned"). No new
marker is introduced: F.5's row form is `| Requirement | Closed by |`, and the
requirement column of a closed row carries no `*(observed)*` qualifier, so the
`*(observed)*` on the F.2 row does not travel with it.

The change that closed it is OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1658
(merged 22 September 2026), which closes
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1645. **Those numbers are in the commit
message rather than in the row**, because every other row in F.5 names the
behaviour and not a change in one implementation's history, and F.6 says why:
"it does not need the implementation to be named — the register describes
behaviour so that it is useful to every implementer facing the same question."
Say the word if the working group would rather the rows cited the change, and
I will add it to this one and to the four already there in the same form.

## What the entry required, and what was verified against the code

The entry's resolution had four parts. Each was checked in the merged tree,
not taken from the change's own description.

- **The step-up is a rule the decision point applies, not a check in a
  handler.** `role_change_via_pipeline` took a `step_up: bool` from its caller,
  which made the handler the gate. It now resolves the elevation itself from
  the caller's live session (`acl::elevation::verified`, which reads the
  session row rather than the bearer token), and `ceremony::decide` applies the
  host invariants after the policy and unconditionally — `StepUpForAdmin`
  (VTI-OPS-051) and `SelfPromotion` (VTI-OPS-050). There is no configuration in
  which they lapse and no policy edit that reaches them.
- **`acl/grant` is gated too**, on the *widening* rather than on the write
  (`elevation::widens_admin_authority`), because a grant writes an entry rather
  than moving one and so has no transition to hang an invariant on. Re-stating
  an entry at the role and scopes it already holds — how the console edits a
  label — confers nothing; re-stating it across more contexts, or across all of
  them, confers authority without the role ever changing, and demands the
  elevation.
- **Nothing was lost in the move.** Self-promotion refusal became the
  invariant; the promote lock moved from the update handler into
  `ceremony::orchestrate`, where the window it closes actually lives; the
  already-an-administrator re-check generalised into a compare-and-swap re-read
  under that lock, so a racing role write is a `409` rather than an overwrite;
  the role-change policy and the role-credential re-mint run on every caller of
  the pipeline.
- **The console promotes through `acl/change-role`** (`PATCH /v1/acl/{did}`
  with `fromRole`/`toRole`), stepping the session up first, and
  **`vtc/members/update` answers `adminRoleForbidden`** — now a *witnessed*
  code in the node's error-code census rather than a declared-but-untested one,
  with the census's unwitnessed count lowered accordingly.

**The related escalation was also fixed, and the closed row records it**,
because it is the part a reader of the register learns most from. The
role-change route never ran `validate_acl_modification`, and the guard it did
run only fired on a subject that was *already* administrative. An entry's
context list means *nowhere* under a non-administrative role and *everywhere*
under an administrative one, so an administrator of one context could take a
member scoped nowhere to the administrative role and land a community-wide
administrator without ever naming a context they do not hold. It is checked
now, decoded through the act-scope reading rather than by testing the list for
emptiness.

## The other two entries are untouched, deliberately

- **The bearer-token entry** (VTI-OPS-020/021/024/093, the 47 tasks served over
  a bearer route with no operation document) is only partly addressed. The
  document dispatcher now enforces, but the routes themselves have not moved.
- **The dispatcher-leniency entry** (VTI-OPS-021/024) was addressed by
  OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1659, and I checked whether it is now
  closed. It is not, quite, and the difference matters:
  - The **acceptance window and the required time of issue are closed
    unconditionally** — a 10-minute window with 60s skew, `issuedAt` required,
    no flag, every binding that reaches the dispatcher.
  - The **proof requirement is enforced unconditionally on the HTTP binding**,
    where there is no transport-authenticated sender to stand in.
  - On the messaging transports it is enforced only when `[trust_tasks]
    require_declared_proof` is set, and that **defaults to false**, because
    `openvtc-core` does not yet sign its documents (OpenVTC/openvtc-core#371).
    While it is off, a proofless document for a task whose definition requires
    a proof is still accepted on those transports from a transport-
    authenticated sender, narrowed to exactly the tasks the entry lists and
    logged at `warn` naming VTI-OPS-021 each time.

  So the divergence is narrowed, bounded and has a stated removal point, but
  the behaviour the entry describes is still reachable in the shipped default.
  That is a different claim from "closed", and the register is only worth
  reading if the two are kept apart — so I have left the entry alone rather
  than closing it, or half-closing it with a qualifier the register does not
  have. It should close when the flag's default flips, and that is one line
  then.

## Render

`npm run render` completes and `docs/index.html` carries the moved row under
F.5 with no trace of it in F.2. No other file changes.

title: Close the admin-promotion entry in the divergence register (#37)
body:
Close the admin-promotion entry in the divergence register (#37)

The entry recorded by #35 leaves F.2 and is recorded in F.5, which is
what the register does with a divergence that has been closed.

Promotion to the administrative role now runs through `acl/change-role`,
and the step-up is a host invariant the decision pipeline applies around
the policy rather than a check in a handler. The elevation is resolved
at the decision point from the caller's live session, so it is a fact
about the caller rather than an assertion by whichever route asked, and
every path onto the same entry is gated by the same one. Self-promotion
is refused by a second invariant. `acl/grant` of the administrative role
checks the same predicate one layer out, on the widening rather than on
the write. The serialisation and the role-change policy moved with the
promotion, the already-administrative re-check generalised into a
compare-and-swap under the same lock, the console was pointed at the
role-change operation, and `vtc/members/update` refuses `role: admin`
with `adminRoleForbidden`, witnessed by the node's error-code census.

Closing it also closed an escalation the entry did not record: the
role-change path never checked the resulting entry against the caller's
own scope, and a context list means nowhere under a non-administrative
role and everywhere under an administrative one, so an administrator of
one context could promote a subject scoped nowhere and land a
community-wide administrator without naming a context they do not hold.
The closed entry carries that, because a reader of the register should
learn what the change turned out to be about.

Closed by OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1658, which closes
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1645. The row itself names
behaviour rather than a change in one implementation's history, as every
other row in F.5 does: the register is written to be useful to every
implementer facing the same question.

The other two entries #35 recorded stay where they are. The bearer-token
entry is only partly addressed, and the dispatcher-leniency entry is
addressed on one binding and behind a flag that defaults to off on the
others, which is not the same as closed.

title: fix(consent): an Approve can no longer be settled as a Deny by its own window closing (VTI-40)
body:
Reported, with a patch, by the Keyring team as **VTI-40**. Thank you: the diagnosis was exact and their `decide()` patch is the core of the popup half below.

## The defect

`confirm.tsx`'s `decide()` sent `RUNTIME_CONSENT_RESULT` without awaiting it and called `window.close()` in the same tick. The background treats the consent window's removal as a denial (`settle(false, …)` from `windows.onRemoved`). Chrome does not order the two events at the service worker, so when the removal arrived first an **Approve was settled as a Deny**, and the result then reached an already-settled consent and was dropped. No error was shown. Every consent surface uses `decide()`: site consent, task consent, the WebAuthn approver, and persona disclosure.

Related: `raiseDisclosureConsent` registered no `onRemoved` at all, so closing a disclosure window left the request pending forever.

## The fix, in two layers

1. **The popup sends, waits for the ack, then closes.** `consent-result.ts` `consentResultSender` awaits the send, swallows errors, then closes. This is Keyring's `Promise.resolve(sendMessage(...)).catch(...).finally(close)`, plus handling for a synchronous throw. It also reports one decision only, because the window now stays up for the round trip and a second click must not send a contradicting answer.
2. **The background acknowledges only after settling.** The result handler calls `deliverConsentResult`, then `sendResponse({ ok: true, matched })`, so the popup's await resolves once the decision has landed.
3. **Close-means-deny waits a grace period (defence in depth).** `consent-window.ts` `openConsentWindow` now owns the create, fail-deny and close-deny lifecycle for all three raisers. On removal it waits `CLOSE_GRACE_MS` (1s) before denying. A microtask or zero timeout would not be enough, because the result is a separate task on the worker's queue. `settle` is idempotent, so a decision that arrives within the grace wins. The grace can only turn a would-be denial into the decision the operator actually sent. Only a result carrying `approved: true` ever approves.
4. **Disclosure consent now settles as a denial on close**, because it goes through the same helper.
5. **Access pane:** the subject DID placeholder now reads `did:key:z6Mk… or did:peer:2…`.

CLAUDE.md gains a short section on the invariant and what breaks it.

## Tests

`tests/consent-window-race.test.mts` (12 tests) uses an in-memory `chrome.windows` stand-in with stepped timers:
- removal before an approve result → **approved**; result then removal → approved
- closed with no decision → **denied** after the grace (pending entry and listener released); a late result cannot overturn it
- **disclosure window closed → denied**
- window creation failure → denied immediately; an unrelated window closing does nothing
- source guard: all three raisers call `openConsentWindow`, `background.ts` has no raw `chrome.windows.create(` or `chrome.windows.onRemoved`, and the result handler calls `sendResponse`
- popup: closes only after the ack, still closes when the send rejects or throws, and sends one decision on a double click

`npm run lint`, `npm test` (777 pass) and `npm run build` in `packages/extension` are all green. There is no version bump because the change is extension-only.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) (n/a, no network)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) (n/a)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) (n/a)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): the consent ack is sent only after settle
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): the `RUNTIME_CONSENT_RESULT` response is internal to the extension and has one consumer
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): a window that could not be opened, or was closed with no decision, still denies
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): if the worker dies during the grace, the in-memory consent dies with it and the caller's promise dies too, as it did before
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none; this closes an R7.2 gap (a lost consent decision)

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.22.1
body:
### Added

- **persona**: Attribute/get — read one attribute, by identifier ([#616](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/616))

The family had no narrow read, and the shape of the workaround is the
  argument for the task. A client revealing one value called
  `persona/attribute/list` with a `typePrefix` and `includeValues`, then
  filtered to the id it already held — so showing one email address
  decrypted and returned every email address the holder has, and the audit
  trail recorded a listing of the pool rather than a decision about one
  fact.

  - Values are withheld unless asked for, and a `sensitivity: high` value
    needs a second flag, on the same two-step as `attribute/list`. A
    withheld value is stated (`valueWithheld`), never left to inference: a
    consumer reading an absent value as "there is none" shows the holder an
    empty field where their passport number is.
  - `version` reads a retained earlier version, which is what makes "what
    did I show them in March" answerable — a disclosure record and a pinned
    entry both name one. A purged version is `versionPurged`, never a
    silent fall back to the current value.
  - `retainedVersions` names the versions still held, so a holder deciding
    whether to purge can see what purging would take away rather than being
    asked to make an irreversible decision blind.

  One identifier, never a list: a maintainer that accepted several would
  recreate the enumeration the task exists to avoid, one call later.

| `trust_tasks` | pub.dev | `0.2.0` → `0.2.1` | patch |

What merging does, per registry (all in `publish.yml`, each keyed on "this
version is not published yet"):

- **crates.io** — `release-plz-release` tags `<crate>-v<version>`, publishes in
  dependency order and creates a GitHub Release per crate. Bump levels come from
  `cargo-semver-checks`.
- **npm** — `publish-npm` publishes with OIDC provenance and tags
  `<prefix>-v<version>`.
- **Go** — `publish-go` builds, vets and tests, then pushes the tag, which *is*
  the publication. **Irreversible**: proxy.golang.org never forgets a tag.
- **pub.dev** — `tag-dart` verifies against the *published* core and pushes the
  tag; `publish-dart.yml` publishes from it.

The npm, Go and Dart bumps are only as accurate as the commit subjects — nothing
checks their APIs the way `cargo-semver-checks` checks the crates. Look for a
missing `!` before merging.

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: security(persona)!: holder authority is granted, never inherited from a role
body:
Closes question 1 of §7 in `docs/05-design-notes/persona-context-first.md`, and records the answers to the other three.

### The defect

`persona-holder` exists because **no role** carries authority over the holder's pool. Super-admin carried it anyway — `authorize` skipped the ACL read for an unrestricted admin and `decide` returned `Ok` unconditionally — which left the capability's premise true only of the roles nobody automates with. The unrestricted admin credential is the one most likely to be sitting in a script, and it read the attribute pool, the faces over it and the disclosure history with no ACL entry saying so.

### The change

The grant is now the only way in, for every role. A super-admin can still grant itself the capability — it is the same credential that grants — so this is not a boundary it cannot cross. It is the difference between crossing it and crossing it **deliberately**: the grant is an ACL write, audited and revocable on its own, where the inherited form left no trace.

The refusal names the fix, per the workspace's error-suggests-the-command rule:

> It requires an ACL entry granted the `persona-holder` capability, and no role carries it — not even super-admin … Grant it deliberately: `pnm acl update --did <did> --capabilities persona-holder`.

### For operators upgrading

`pnm acl update --did <did> --capabilities persona-holder`, or `pnm contexts create --admin-holder` when provisioning a client that is the holder's own. The provisioning paths already carry an existing grant across a credential rollover, and `create_acl` already refuses a context-scoped admin from minting one — neither needed changing.

### Tests

The 30 integration tests that broke were the defect on display: the fixture authenticated as an unrestricted admin and reached the pool. It now grants the capability explicitly, `authed` alone is what an ungranted caller looks like, and `the_grant_reaches_the_pool_and_nothing_else_does` holds both halves — including that the refusal names the capability.

One test needed a second identity (`OTHER_SEED`): it needs a granted holder and an ungranted caller *at the same moment*, and a grant is keyed by DID. SPEC §7.2 item 6 refuses a document whose issuer disagrees with the transport identity, so the second caller signs with its own seed rather than borrowing the holder's.

### Also

§7 of the design note is rewritten from four open questions into four decisions with their reasoning — including that ratifying the agent-scoped correlation index surfaced a live probe oracle on `persona/local/profile/put`, closed in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#609.

CI set run locally: fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, workspace tests (4819), `-p vtc-service -p vtc-client` (1865).
